☆ Copying along Arithmetic Progressions Cannot Simulate Interleaving with Polylogarithmic Loss
Matthias G. Mayer
Two classical ways to compress a word are straight-line programs (SLPs), which build it by concatenating smaller pieces, and the Lempel-Ziv 77 (LZ77) factorisation, which copies earlier parts of it; their sizes are measures of repetitiveness. LZ77 approximates the smallest SLP efficiently: it has no more factors than a smallest SLP has size, and yields an SLP at most a logarithmic factor larger in near-linear time. Motivated by online prediction, Kosoy introduced zipline programs, which are analogous to SLPs but interleave their pieces round-robin instead of concatenating them. Her generalisation of LZ77, the arithmetic repetition system, describes a word by copies from one arithmetic progression of positions to a later one. Do arithmetic repetition systems approximate the smallest zipline program as well? Kosoy proved that the least size $\mathrm{ARC}(x)$ of an arithmetic repetition system for a word $x$ of length $n$ is at most a factor $O(n^{1/3})$ larger than the least size $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ of a zipline program for it, and asked whether this factor is tight. Her polynomial-time next-letter predictor makes $O(\mathrm{ARC}(x)\log n)$ mistakes, so a polylogarithmic factor would bound its mistakes by $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$, which no known polynomial-time predictor achieves. We show that the optimal exponent is $1/4$, not $1/3$: $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \le 2n^{1/4}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ for every word $x$, and at every large enough length $n$ some binary word has $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \ge n^{1/4-o(1)}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$.

☆ Speed-Robust Scheduling for Total Completion Time
Moritz Buchem, Nicole Megow, Morten Weber
We study two-stage speed-robust scheduling for minimizing total completion time. Jobs must be partitioned into $M$ bags before an adversary reveals the speeds of at most $M$ machines. Each bag is then assigned to one available machine, and the jobs on each machine may be processed in any order independent of the bags. We compare with an optimal schedule that knows the speeds in advance and assigns jobs individually. This model has been studied for makespan minimization. We initiate its study for total completion time, as suggested by Stein and Zhong (TALG 2020). For an unknown number of identical machines, we show that the optimal deterministic robustness factor is exactly~$13/12$, both for unit-size jobs and for arbitrary processing times. For infinitesimally small jobs, the factor lies between $31/30\approx1.0333$ and $28/27\approx1.0370$, well below the optimal makespan factor of about $1.2071$. General speeds make the problem strictly harder: no deterministic algorithm is better than $1.2669$-robust, already for infinitesimally small jobs. We give a $25/16$-robust algorithm for arbitrary processing times and improve the guarantee to $1681/1152\approx1.4592$ for infinitesimally small jobs. Our main tools are a layer decomposition that extends guarantees from unit-size jobs to arbitrary processing times when one assignment satisfies them for every prefix in non-increasing processing-time order, and a threshold analysis of the bag counts produced by greedy assignment rules.
☆ Improved Approximation for Weighted $k$-Set Packing via a Simple Two-Phase Approach
Mehrshad Taziki, Rico Zenklusen
Weighted $k$-set packing asks for a maximum-weight collection of pairwise disjoint sets, each of cardinality at most $k$. For every fixed $k\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm with approximation factor $\left(1- 1/{\sqrt3} \right)k+O(\log k) \approx 0.4226k + O(\log k)$, improving the previous best factor of $0.4621k + O(\sqrt{k})$ through a simple two-phase approach. In a first phase, our algorithm constructs a packing by processing random weight buckets of varying widths with an unweighted packing algorithm. We show that a small expected weight of this packing relative to the optimum forces a large expected total surplus in the optimum. Surplus quantifies the potential for improving a packing through star swaps. In the second phase, we solve and round a configuration LP to turn sufficiently large surplus into an increase in expected weight. Our procedure can easily be derandomized.
☆ When is Uniform Sampling Optimal? Coresets for Distributional Clustering
Junqiu Hu, Lingxiao Huang, Baoduo Xu
Recent work [1] settled the optimal worst-case strong $\varepsilon$-coreset size for Euclidean $k$-means in unrestricted dimension at $\tildeΘ(\min\{k^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-2}, k\varepsilon^{-4}\})$, showing that the natural target $\tilde{O}(k\varepsilon^{-2})$ is unattainable in general. For mixtures of $k$ isotropic Gaussian components with balanced weights and bounded scale imbalance in dimension $d\ge\log k$, we show that uniform sampling yields strong $\varepsilon$-coresets of size $\tilde{O}(k\varepsilon^{-2})$, without cluster separation. This saves a factor of $\min\{\sqrt{k},\varepsilon^{-2}\}$ over the worst-case bound, up to logarithms. For population approximation by independent, equally weighted samples, the near-linear rate is optimal up to logarithmic factors over this class. More generally, for datasets generated from an isotropic Gaussian mixture $μ$ satisfying a mild cost-comparison assumption, uniform sampling yields strong $\varepsilon$-coresets of size $\tilde{O}((kζ_μ+π_{\min}^{-1})\varepsilon^{-2})$, where $π_{\min}$ is the minimum component weight and $ζ_μ$ measures scale imbalance. Our proof uses a base-shift cost decomposition: one query center per component describes the base costs, and graph spanners control the sparse corrections from points switching centers. For general mixtures under cost and tail assumptions, we obtain $\tilde{O}((kζ_μ+π_{\min}^{-1})\varepsilon^{-2}\min\{\sqrt{k},\varepsilon^{-2}\})$ samples. We also prove a matching $\tildeΩ(\min\{k^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-2},k\varepsilon^{-4}\})$ lower bound for population approximation by uniform sampling from anisotropic Gaussian mixtures, even with equal weights and a shared covariance matrix. [1] Junqiu Hu, Lingxiao Huang, Jian Li, and Baoduo Xu. Tight coreset bounds for $(k, z)$-clustering in Euclidean and doubling metrics, 2026. arXiv:2610.34373.
☆ Rounded Potentials Certify Exact Maximum Flow
Ohad Trabelsi
The textbook certificate for maximum flow is lopsided: the cut takes one bit per vertex, while the flow takes one number per edge. Indeed, some graphs have $Θ(n^2)$ terminal pairs for which every maximum flow uses $Θ(n^2)$ edges. Yet we show that one short number per vertex suffices for both cut and flow: $n$ vertex potentials, each rounded to $O(\log(nW))$ bits, certify the exact maximum $st$-flow value in any directed graph with integer capacities at most $W$. Exact potentials can have exponentially large representations. Rounding them may violate flow conservation, but the total error across any cut is less than one unit, so integrality of cut capacities absorbs it. Checking conservation is local and linear in the capacities, allowing the same certificate to yield new bounds in four models (capacities are polynomially bounded unless stated otherwise): - Online annotated streaming. $\widetilde{O}(n)$ total cost (help plus space) for the maximum $st$-flow value, optimal up to logarithmic factors, answering a question of Thaler (ICALP 2016) on whether $o(n^2)$ is possible. - Broadcast proof-labeling. $O(\log(n+p))$-bit labels certifying a maximum $st$-flow value of $p$ in directed and undirected graphs with arbitrary capacities, optimal for $p\ge n^{Ω(1)}$, settling that regime of a question of Korman, Kutten, and Peleg (Distributed Computing 2010). - Merlin-Arthur verification. $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ time and $O(n^3\log n)$ proof length for directed All-Pairs Max-Flow, improving on previous verification times of $n^{4+o(1)}$ for general capacities and $n^{3.5+o(1)}$ for unit capacities, and answering a question of Akmal (TheoretiCS 2024). - Nondeterministic algorithms. $O(n^{3.614})$ time for directed All-Pairs Max-Flow, or $n^{3.5+o(1)}$ if $ω=2$: the first subquartic bound for general edge capacities, answering a question of Trabelsi (SODA 2025).
☆ Online and Fully-Dynamic Sorting
Yossi Azar, Sujoy Bhore, Devdan Dey, Debmalya Panigrahi, Or Vardi, Ian Zhang
Online sorting asks how to place $n$ sequentially arriving elements in an array to minimize the sum of absolute differences between consecutive elements. Fully-dynamic sorting further extends the problem to allow both element insertions and deletions. Without recourse, these problems face strong lower bounds on the competitive ratio: $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ for online sorting and $Ω(n)$ for fully-dynamic sorting. In sharp contrast, we show that allowing only poly-logarithmic recourse yields at least exponential improvements in the competitive ratio for both problems:(1) Our main algorithmic result is a deterministic fully-dynamic sorting algorithm that is $O(\log^2 n)$-competitive and has $O(\log^4 n)$ amortized recourse per update. We complement this with a lower bound showing that any deterministic algorithm with any $O(\mathrm{polylog}(n))$ competitive ratio has amortized recourse at least $Ω(\sqrt{\log n})$.(2) For the insertion-only setting, we establish a family of approximation--recourse tradeoffs, including $O(\log\log n)$ competitive ratio with $O(\log\log n)$ amortized recourse. Given the lower bound in the fully-dynamic case, this result shows that the insertion-only problem yields exponentially better bounds than the fully-dynamic one.(3) Finally, we show that the stronger approximation-recourse tradeoff for the insertion-only case extends to the fully-dynamic setting when the array has $(1+\varepsilon)n$ space.
☆ Minimum Sum-of-Radii Clustering with Strong and Weak Oracles
Zachary Friggstad, Mahya Jamshidian, Ali Vakilian
In the minimum sum of radii (MSR) problem, the input is a set of $n$ points in a metric space and a parameter $k$, and the goal is to cover the points by at most $k$ balls, each centered at an input point, while minimizing the sum of their radii. We study MSR in the weak-strong oracle model of Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram, and Wang (COLT'24), where the metric is unknown and is accessed through two oracles. The answers of the weak oracle are given to us for free: for every pair of points, we receive a distance value that, with probability $δ$, is arbitrarily corrupted. Exact distances are available only through costly strong queries, where a strong query on a point reveals its exact distances to all previously strongly queried points, and the goal is to minimize the number of strong queries. For every constant $δ< 1/2$, we give the first polynomial-time algorithm that makes $O(k \log n \log\log n)$ strong point queries and, with high probability, returns an $O(1)$-approximation for MSR; the previously best algorithm required running time and a number of strong queries exponential in $k$. This is within an $O(\log\log n)$ factor of a lower bound that we prove: any constant-factor approximation that succeeds with high probability on every instance must make $Ω(k \log n)$ strong queries in expectation on some instance. The same $Ω(k \log n)$ lower bound holds for $k$-center, where it matches the known upper bound up to an $O(\log\log n)$ factor. An optimal MSR cluster can be small both in size and in radius, so a uniform sample of strongly queried points may miss it entirely. Instead, our algorithm uses a packing LP over the balls certified so far to decide which points to query next. The analysis holds against an adversary who knows which pairs are corrupted.

☆ Beyond 4: Improved Competitive Traveling Repairperson
Bibek Maharjan, Gokarna Sharma
With $k\geq 1$ repairpersons starting initially from a depot, we present a 3.877-competitive deterministic algorithm for the fundamental online traveling repairperson problem on an arbitrary metric. For the special class of zero-residual instances, we improve the ratio to $3+ε$ for every $ε>0$. We also extend these results to some variants of the related so-called online dial-a-ride problem. The state-of-the-art is the 4-competitive deterministic algorithm for both problems.

♻ ☆ Estimating Random-Walk Probabilities in Directed Graphs
Christian Bertram, Mads Vestergaard Jensen, Mikkel Thorup, Hanzhi Wang, Shuyi Yan
We study discounted random walks in directed graphs. In each step, the walk either terminates with a constant probability $α$, or proceeds to a random out-neighbor. Our goal is to estimate the probability $π(s, t)$ that a discounted random walk starting from $s$ terminates at $t$. This probability is also known as the Personalized PageRank (PPR) score, which measures the relevance of $t$ to $s$, for instance, when $s$ and $t$ are web pages on the Internet. We aim to estimate $π(s, t)$ within a constant relative error with constant probability. A variety of algorithms have been developed for several problem variants, such as single-pair, single-source, single-target, and single-node estimation, under both worst-case and average-case settings, and for different combinations of allowed graph queries. However, in many important cases, there remain polynomial gaps between known upper and lower bounds. In this paper, we establish tight bounds for all problem variants and query combinations, closing all existing gaps in both the worst-case and average-case settings. We provide tight (up to logarithmic factors) lower bounds, showing that for all but one query combination, existing algorithms are already optimal. For the remaining case, we design a novel algorithm that matches our new lower bound up to logarithmic factors, thereby nearly achieving optimality. This is the first algorithm to exploit this specific query combination. It uses a new randomized bidirectional framework that combines randomized backward propagation with selective Monte Carlo estimation.

♻ ☆ Tunnels: Compressing the Solution Subgraph of Regular Path Queries
Adrián Gómez-Brandón, Gonzalo Navarro
Regular path queries (RPQs) are increasingly expected to return the paths that match them, not only their endpoints. Since the number of matching paths can be exponential or infinite, a standard way to deliver them (PMR) is the subgraph $\Hs$ of the product between the graph and the query automaton that contains exactly the nodes lying on some solution path. We show that $\Hs$ can be compressed much further when the graph is available to the decoder: most of $\Hs$ can be regenerated by re-running small parts of the traversal, and only the places where the traversal would waste significant effort on dead branches need to be stored. We formalize this as \emph{tunnels}: regions of $\Hs$ that are re-expanded from a stored entry point with a bounded amount of extra work, either an absolute budget or one proportional to the output produced. We handle the three classes of RPQs: constant-to-variable, constant-to-constant, and variable-to-variable. In the latter, we study the combination of tunnels with cutting the query at a selective articulation point of the automaton and encoding the answer as a union of Cartesian products of leftward and rightward traversals. Our experimental results show improvements of 2 to 3 orders of magnitude over the baseline space of PMR, for an acceptable increase in traversal time.
♻ ☆ On the enumeration of signatures of XOR-CNF's
Nadia Creignou, Oscar Defrain, Frédéric Olive, Simon Vilmin
Given a CNF formula $\varphi$ with clauses $C_1, \dots, C_m$ over a set of variables $V$, a truth assignment $\mathbf{a} : V \to \{0, 1\}$ generates a binary sequence $σ_\varphi(\mathbf{a})=(C_1(\mathbf{a}), \ldots, C_m(\mathbf{a}))$, called a signature of $\varphi$, where $C_i(\mathbf{a})=1$ if clause $C_i$ evaluates to 1 under assignment $\mathbf{a}$, and $C_i(\mathbf{a})=0$ otherwise. Signatures and their associated generation problems have given rise to new yet promising research questions in algorithmic enumeration. In a recent paper, Bérczi et al. interestingly proved that generating signatures of a CNF is tractable despite the fact that verifying a solution is hard. They also showed the hardness of finding maximal signatures of an arbitrary CNF due to the intractability of satisfiability in general. Their contribution leaves open the problem of efficiently generating maximal signatures for tractable classes of CNFs, i.e., those for which satisfiability can be solved in polynomial time. Stepping into that direction, we completely characterize the complexity of generating all, minimal, and maximal signatures for XOR-CNFs.

♻ ☆ Contrastive Identification and Generation in the Limit NeurIPS 2026
Xiaoyu Li, Andi Han, Jiaojiao Jiang, Junbin Gao
In identification in the limit (Gold, 1967), a learner reads positive examples and must eventually name the target hypothesis; in generation in the limit (Kleinberg and Mullainathan, 2024), it must eventually produce new positive examples. We study a weaker, relational signal: each observation is an unordered pair $\{x,y\}$ with $h(x)\neq h(y)$, such as a cannot-link constraint or a dissimilar-pair label, and the learner never learns which point is positive. All our results come from one object: a pair is valid for every member of a finite family exactly when its points lie in antipodal cells of the family's membership map. (1) For every corruption budget $k$, known or unknown, we characterize exactly the identifiable classes. Incomparable hypotheses must cover the domain and share more than $2k$ points, and Angluin's tell-tale sets must survive the loss of $2k$ points. Every unbounded budget makes any two hypotheses confusable. (2) A contrastive closure dimension characterizes uniform generation. On finite classes, generation fails exactly when a family that shares a presentation has a finite common support; on countable classes this finite condition no longer suffices. (3) On clean data the four learning criteria form a strict diamond. (4) Under corruption the order changes: some classes are identifiable from contrastive pairs under every finite budget by one algorithm, but not from positive examples with one corrupted example.
comment: Extended version of a NeurIPS 2026 paper. 42 pages, 9 figures
♻ ☆ On the Price of Privacy for Language Identification and Generation NeurIPS 2026
Xiaoyu Li, Andi Han, Jiaojiao Jiang, Junbin Gao
Large language models train on sensitive user data, so we ask what differential privacy (DP) costs in language learning. We study private language identification and generation in the agnostic statistical setting. For identification, privacy is free: at every fixed $\varepsilon$, pure DP and $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP with $δ\ge n^{-O(1)}$ keep the non-private rate $\exp(-r(n))$ for every $r(n)=o(n)$. For generation, the price depends on what is public. With a public witness bound, pure DP loses at most a factor $Θ(\min\{1,\varepsilon\})$ in the exponent, and on suitable two-language collections the optimal rate is $\exp(-Θ(\min\{1,\varepsilon\}\,n))$. Without such a bound, pure DP can lose the exponential rate itself, already for two languages: every rate $\exp(-o(n))$ stays achievable, but no exponential rate is. On these collections, $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP keeps an exponential rate if and only if $\log(1/δ)=o(n)$. Three facts about pure DP drive the proofs. It turns a robustness margin into an exponentially small error. It obeys a private form of Le Cam's two-point bound. And it cannot see the absence of a string.

♻ ☆ Exact Algorithms for Edge Deletion to Cactus
Sheikh Shakil Akhtar, Geevarghese Philip
We study two related problems on simple, un-directed graphs: Edge Deletion to Cactus and Spanning Tree to Cactus. Edge Deletion to Cactus has been known to be NP-hard on general graphs at least since 1988. We show improved exact algorithms for the former and a polynomial time algorithm for the latter.
♻ ☆ The Quick and the Dead: Estimating Sparse-Matrix Permanents with Adaptive Work Filtering
Deniz Elbek, Yiğit Manafi, Zeynep Gürdal, Sinan Yıldırım, Kamer Kaya
Rasmussen's permanent estimator is a simple and unbiased estimator for the permanent of a binary matrix, but its practical performance can be limited by trajectories that terminate before completing a perfect matching. These failed trajectories, together with dispersion among the surviving weights, can substantially reduce the effective sample size. Although the literature leverages techniques such as doubly-stochastic matrix scaling to improve proposal balance and support filtering to remove structurally infeasible choices, using these at every step can substantially increase the trajectory cost. Furthermore, these techniques do not directly address the choice of the next vertex whose residual neighborhood is used for the proposal. This paper uses the classical minimum-degree ordering in sparse matrix algorithms to select the next vertex with $\mathcal{O}(n + m)$ total bucket-maintenance work per trajectory, where $n$ is the number of rows/columns in the matrix and $m$ is the number of nonzeros. The proposed estimator uses adaptive schedules to invoke the more expensive scaling and filtering operations only when needed. The experiments show favorable empirical accuracy under fixed time budgets on the tested matrices.
♻ ☆ Regular Expression Matching with Ordered Linear Backreferences
Philip Bille, Inge Li Gørtz, Rikke Schjeldrup Jessen
A regular expression with backreferences (rewb) specifies a set of strings formed by characters combined with concatenation, union, star operators, and backreferences. A backreference consists of a capturing group $(\cdot)_i$ and one or more references $\backslash i$. The substring matched by the reference must match the same substring that was matched by the corresponding capturing group. We focus on a subclass, which we call ordered linear rewbs where the references and capturing groups occur only outside star and union operators. Furthermore, we require that all references to a capturing group occur before the next capturing group in the rewb. In full generality, rewb matching is NP-complete, but efficient solutions exist for various subclasses. For linear rewbs with one capturing group and $k$ references, Uezato~[CPM 2026] gave an $O(k n^2 m^2)$ time and $O(n^2m^2)$ space algorithm, where $m$ is the length of the regular expression $R$ and $n$ is the length of the string $Q$. For the special case of $k=1$, Nogami and Terauchi~[MFCS 2025] gave an $O(n^2m^2)$ time and $O(n+ m^2)$ space algorithm. On the other hand, Nogami, Nakamura, and Terauchi~[arXiv 2026] gave a conditional lower bound, showing that we cannot solve the problem in $O(n^{2-ε} \mathrm{poly}(m))$ for any $ε> 0$ assuming the orthogonal vector hypothesis. Our main result is a new improved algorithm that runs in $O(n^2m+n^2k\log n)$ time and uses $O(nm)$ space, and handles the more general case of ordered linear rewbs with multiple capturing groups.

♻ ☆ Training Multi-Layer Over-Parametrized Neural Network in Subquadratic Time
Zhao Song, Lichen Zhang, Ruizhe Zhang
We consider the problem of training the last layer of a multi-layer over-parametrized neural network to minimize the empirical risk induced by a loss function. In the typical setting of over-parametrization, the network width $m$ is much larger than the data dimension $d$ and the number of training samples $n$ ($m=\mathrm{poly}(n,d)$), which induces a prohibitively large weight matrix $W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ per layer above the first. Naively, when the layer inputs are dense, one has to pay $O(m^2)$ time to read the weight matrix and evaluate the neural network function in both forward and backward computation. To reduce the training cost per iteration, we propose a framework that uses $O(m^2nL)$ time in the initialization phase and achieves a truly subquadratic amortized cost per iteration in terms of $m$, i.e., $m^{2-Ω(1)}$ per iteration. The speedup comes from a sparse activation, a shifted ReLU whose threshold at each layer is proportional to the norm of the layer input. With this threshold every layer is positively homogeneous, so our convergence proof needs a width only polynomial in the depth $L$, in $n$ and in the inverse smallest kernel eigenvalues. The inputs of the trained layer are fixed and sparse. In this setting, simpler algorithms without a data structure reach the same cost per iteration, and maintaining the products of the last layer with its inputs lowers it to $mn^{ω-1+o(1)}$, where $ω$ is the matrix multiplication exponent. Our result can be viewed as an idealized model of maintaining a small amount of state on top of a frozen pre-trained model to speed up fine-tuning, a core procedure to deploy large language models (LLMs). Our guarantees assume that the frozen layers are random, and for a pre-trained model only the cost per iteration of maintaining these products carries over.
comment: ITCS 2024. This version corrects the analysis: the threshold of each layer now scales with the norm of the layer input, which removes a factor exponential in the depth from the width, and the claims are narrowed to training the last layer at an amortized cost per iteration. It also adds simpler and faster algorithms for this setting
♻ ☆ Tight Lower Bounds for Differentially Private Continual Counting
Charlie Harrison, Ethan Leeman
The Binary Tree Mechanism is a standard algorithm for differentially private continual counting, but its complete asymptotic optimality under differential privacy has remained unresolved since its introduction. We resolve this question. For $0 \leq \varepsilon \leq 1$, we prove asymptotically tight lower bounds for $\ell_\infty$, mean squared, and maximum per-coordinate expected squared error simultaneously under all regimes of $0 \leq δ\leq 1/4$. These bounds hold for arbitrary mechanisms, even when the entire stream is available in advance. Our lower bounds match the (blocked) Binary Tree Mechanism instantiated with the best of Laplace or Gaussian noise, establishing its asymptotic optimality. Our proof uses a single hard distribution where elements are ``tagged'' as potentially being the target flipped element via a score evaluated down a tree. A simple modification of the score allows the same framework to establish tight lower bounds for all three error measures.
♻ ☆ Bounded Local Generator Classes for Deterministic State Evolution
R. Jay Martin
Persistent memory must retain history without revisiting it at every transition. Bounded Local Generator Classes (BLGC) formalize carried numerical state, selected context and ordered local updates. The $\ell^\infty$ formulation permits countably many uniformly bounded coordinates without square summability. Projected maps preserve admissibility, Lipschitz estimates control finite-horizon sensitivity, and bounded acquisition and evaluation give a cardinality-independent transition-work contract. OPAL supplies a working persistent-state engine and controlled production measurements. After six successful million-node workloads, 18 matched fresh Release processes compared original and incremental receipt indexing at 10,000, 100,000 and 1,000,000 nodes. Degree, record shape, state dimension, active-target count and event schedule were fixed. Repaired resident-update P50 remained 0.083-0.084 microseconds; subsequent receipt-event P50 ranged from 4.458 to 6.459 microseconds across all scales. The original receipt path took 177.700-182.297 milliseconds at one million nodes. Reliability was tested alongside performance. Baseline and repaired engines produced byte-identical checkpoints, including continuation after fresh-process recovery. Replay, conflict, rejection, concurrent-event and allocation-failure checks passed; all 18 matched scaling processes passed their correctness gates. The repair preserves the state law and durable receipt format. Finally, we analyze the polarization state of the sky across different times and weather conditions, and demonstrate its practical impact on a downstream shape-from-polarization task.

A closed-credit ledger makes credit a collision invariant and unlocks acoustic waves at a measurable, engineerable speed; a zero-sum projection gate conserves centroid momentum unconditionally, for any proposal stream. Both layers are proven and executed: the axis total is conserved to the digit over 66 interventions under a live gate, and the pre-registered decisive probe returns the theory's directional verdict: linear wavefronts where the ledger holds, dissipation where it does not, replicated across two population sizes. For agents that must never stop, the gas description is not a metaphor: it is the measurement interface through which their future becomes readable.

Across processors, a hybrid pipeline balances selections between the CPU and the GPU before grouped decoding under bounded memory. To use 3D K-hedral tilings in practice, they need to satisfy two requirements. To guide the part-level partitioning, we propose a new graph representation with regular structures to facilitate the generation of tiles with identical shapes while ensuring that they are interlocking. Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.

Each succeeds with one or two targeted faults (lower bounds under the emulation-based setting). These results show that CHERI's guarantees depend on the physical integrity of capability metadata, the uninterrupted execution of metadata checks, and the integrity of the revocation bitmap: a single targeted fault can circumvent spatial safety, temporal safety, or control-flow integrity. CHERI still raises the cost of exploitation, since fault injection is a prerequisite for every attack and the sentry mechanism forces an attacker to supply a valid tagged capability or spend a second fault restoring the tag. Based on these findings, we propose mitigations: ECC-protected capability memory, capability field authentication codes, redundant execution of security-critical checks, and revocation bitmap integrity verification.

Experiments show how resource limits, address interleaving, fragment arrival patterns, and scheduling policies affect write completion and request latency. The results highlight the need to consider resource limits and scheduling policies jointly, accounting for their interactions with write assembly and read eligibility. We also integrate HBF-EventLab with real GPU execution of Qwen3-0.6B, combining profiled GPU activity durations with simulated weight-access delays to estimate time to first token and time per output token, with logits and output tokens remaining bitwise identical to those from native GPU execution. However, despite reduced operand precision, accumulation is often retained at high floating-point precisions, leaving a substantial hardware cost that operand quantization alone does not address. In particular, systolic arrays, as used in tensor accelerators such as Google TPU and AWS Trainium, distribute accumulation across distinct processing elements but conventionally use uniform accumulator precision throughout the array. This spatial organization offers an opportunity to reduce hardware cost by tailoring precision to individual accumulation stages. In this work, we present MIAO, a hardware-software co-design framework that jointly selects product precision and stage-dependent accumulator widths to minimize hardware area and energy cost under an end-to-end perplexity constraint. MIAO first calibrates MX block-scale shifts to reduce intermediate magnitudes while preserving operand quantization accuracy, then assigns narrower accumulators to earlier stages and progressively wider accumulators to later stages. To efficiently explore the resulting design space, MIAO combines hardware cost estimates derived from logic synthesis with a calibrated accuracy predictor to identify promising precision configurations, then validates the accuracy of promising candidates through bit-exact end-to-end LLM evaluation. Across MXFP8, MXFP6, and MXFP4, MIAO reduces processing element (PE) array area by up to 38.7% and energy by up to 36.1% relative to the all-BF16 accumulation baseline, with at most 1.60% additional perplexity degradation over operand-only MX quantization across six LLMs.

FCP separates conformance (does the artifact satisfy a formal reading of a requirement?), which model checkers and SMT solvers decide, from fidelity (does the reading mean what the prose means?), which has no decision procedure but is refutable by a concrete witness. Eight ways a proof can falsely certify a requirement each become a mechanical check that returns a witness, and what no machine can settle becomes concrete questions for the request's author. Adapters place hardware, text, agents and code on the same engines. On four hardware designs, trusting AI-written assertions certified 23% of violated requirements, and FCP certified none. On ten code tasks, code from three language models passed its own tests and violated the request every time. Trusting the tests certified all 33 violations, and FCP certified three. Agreement among models, readings or tests did not imply correctness.

Many quantum algorithms rely on Boolean functions, which must therefore be implemented reversibly within quantum circuits. Reversible circuit synthesis provides a way to translate such Boolean functions into reversible circuits. Binary decision diagrams (BDDs) offer a scalable approach to this task, but the resulting BDDs and circuits depend heavily on variable ordering. Candidate heuristics directly manipulate variable orderings using standard BDD operations and are selected by downstream QCC. Across the benchmark set, HGA-QE achieves a 70.9\% tie-or-win rate against the per-function best baseline and is strictly best on 13.5\% of the functions. The results demonstrate broadly competitive QCC performance, with HGA-QE showing a clearer relative advantage in strict wins on the two benchmark suites drawn from sources different from the data used for heuristic discovery.

Methods using explicit 4D distributions, keyframe interpolation, or anchor binding share two GPU data-movement bottlenecks. Polymorphic PIM adapts a shared near-memory datapath to representation-specific field layouts and selection procedures. It filters and compacts valid data into contiguous inputs before the GPU accesses complete attributes, reducing ineffective transfers. Multi-Frame Rendering Dataflow reuses active attributes and stable depth relationships within a temporal window, reducing repeated work across frames. Hybrid Dataflow Scheduling overlaps near-memory data preparation with GPU rendering to reduce waiting. Across three 4DGS methods and six dynamic scenes, GSPIM achieves a 4.15x geometric-mean speedup and a 4.99x geometric-mean energy-efficiency improvement over a fully optimized frame-by-frame GPU baseline. The maximum scene-level PSNR difference is 0.011 dB, and the added physical footprint is 18.7172 square millimeters across 32 LPDDR5 dies.

Starting from curriculum supervised fine-tuning (SFT), RWOPD distills CodeV-SVA-14B into a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct student. The student has the highest reported pass@1, pass@5, and pass@10 on NL2SVA-Human and NL2SVA-Machine among the compared models, including specialized baselines and 671B general-purpose models.

♻ ☆ Is Agentic AI Ready for Real-World Hardware Engineering? A Deep Dive with Phoenix-bench NeurIPS 2026

We ask whether agentic AI systems built for software engineering transfer to realistic hardware engineering. Existing hardware LLM benchmarks isolate sub-tasks but none jointly requires repository navigation, hierarchy-aware localization, Electronic Design Automation (EDA) executable verification, and maintenance-style patching. We introduce \textbf{Phoenix-bench}, a synchronized corpus of 511 verified Verilator instances from 114 GitHub repositories, each shipped with the developer patch, design-flow labels, fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass testbenches, and a Docker-pinned EDA environment so resolved-rate differences reflect agent behavior rather than toolchain availability. Using Phoenix-bench we run a uniform evaluation of four commercial agents and eight open-source agentic structures across four LLM backbones, plus two diagnostic interventions (file-level oracle localization and one round of testbench-log feedback). Three findings emerge. (i)~Software and hardware are fundamentally different engineering tasks: the same agent loses 37\% to 58\% from SWE-bench Verified to Phoenix-bench because hardware bugs propagate across parallel instantiated modules through signal flow rather than along a software-style call graph, and software-tuned agents stop at the symptom file instead of tracing back through the instantiation chain. (ii)~Failures concentrate on design control-flow / finite state machine (FSM) bugs, verification testbench bugs, and hard cases that demand cross-hierarchy signal-flow tracking and coordinated multi-file edits. (iii)~Localization granularity matters far more than localization itself: a perfect file-level oracle yields only $+1.4$\% because the agent then breaks files that did not need editing, while a single round of test case feedback lifts resolved rate by $42$\% to $45$\% because the test case tells \emph{where} the bug is and \emph{what} the fix has to look like.

☆ Type-Confusion Security

Type systems are a lightweight way to obtain formal assurance that code upholds security properties. However, decentralized systems, such as smart contracts and Model Context Protocol ecosystems, have limited ability to constrain the behavior of untrusted code. In such systems, attackers may attempt to confuse trusted code by supplying values that do not behave according to their advertised types, an attack that we call type confusion. Well-known attacks such as confused deputy attacks, reentrancy attacks, and control-flow hijacking can be understood as instances of type confusion. We define type confusion security as the property that unrestricted attackers who need not follow the type system have no more power than limited attackers who fully obey it. We formally define type confusion security as a real--ideal emulation, and in the context of an information-flow-typed core calculus that statically enforces security against well-typed attackers, prove that its run-time checks also enforce security against ill-typed attackers. In this system, programmers can write code while reasoning about security only against well-typed attackers; the security guarantees enforced by the type system still hold. We mechanize a proof of type confusion security in Lean.

GraphPass encodes each CFG with a graph attention (GAT) or graph convolutional (GCN) encoder and classifies it into one of the five sequences. On a synthetic benchmark of 5,000 generated CFGs in five program families, both encoders agree with the benchmark's reference label on about 92% of held-out programs, versus 68.4% for a hand-written rule-based heuristic and 85% for a flat MLP. An edge ablation indicates that this gain comes from per-block processing rather than from CFG edges: a GCN given the same basic-block features with all edges removed scores 95.0%, versus 92.2% with the true CFG. In this benchmark the label is determined by the program family, so the task amounts to family recognition. Real-compiler speedup is not measured. Inference costs O(|V| + |E|) per CFG, measured at 1.7 ms for a typical program and about 0.8 s for a 100,000-block graph on one CPU core.

To address this challenge, we introduce Proxima, a highly effective automated SEC scheduling framework guided by a distance-related metric termed proximity. Defined directly on the detector error model (DEM), proximity quantifies the minimum number of additional faults required to complete a seed fault to an undetectable logical failure, naturally capturing arbitrary circuit-level fault mechanisms and bounding $d_{\mathrm{circ}}$ from above. Proxima synthesizes a pool of valid schedules at a target depth and ranks them by evaluating proximity within small, graph-local DEM fault subsets, progressively enlarging the subset only to break ties among top-ranked candidates. Across a broad spectrum of qLDPC code families, Proxima consistently attains low circuit depths and high circuit-level distance bounds, reducing LER by 1.4--2.6$\times$ over the strongest automated baseline and up to $40\times$ over others while generalizing robustly across noise models and decoders. Furthermore, by exploiting translational symmetry via a compact monomial representation, Proxima discovers depth-8 uniform schedules for bivariate bicycle codes that surpass even IBM's depth-7 reference schedule [Nature, 2024] by 2.1--5.1$\times$, establishing the DEM-level proximity as a practical objective for fault-tolerant compilation.

We define the $S_hR_k$-process that generalizes the notion of Hamiltonicity through the lense of information diffusion. We say that a graph is $S_hR_k$-infectable if it can be fully infected by transmission trees seeded by at most $h$ initial infections in which each infection leads to at most $k$ others; or, equivalently, if it can be exactly vertex-covered by at most $h$ trees of degree at most $k$. While determining $S_hR_k$ infectability is NP-hard in general, we argue fixed-parameter tractability when parameterised by treewidth. Additionally, we give computational experimental results comparing the performance of several natural heuristics for minimising the number of initial infections required to an optimal LP-based approach on several standard complex network models. We find that a uniformly random approach outperforms greedy heuristics based on degree or clustering.

For every $ε>0$, we give an algorithm with recourse $O(ε^{-2})$ whose reported set has, at every time, expected value at least $1/4-ε$ times the largest value of a feasible set of arrived elements. The algorithm evaluates the function polynomially often, and only on sets of arrived elements. We also show that no algorithm with constant recourse achieves a ratio above $1/4$, even if it knows the function and the arrival order in advance and has unlimited computation, and that any fixed ratio above $1/4$ requires recourse that grows as a positive power of the cardinality budget. Thus $1/4$ is the optimal limiting ratio with constant recourse. The previous best ratio with constant recourse was $3-2\sqrt2\approx0.172$. Our algorithm assigns selection probabilities of at most one half and maintains, as elements arrive, an inequality bounding the value of every feasible set by a multiple of the expected value of a random set drawn with these probabilities; the reported set moves to a rounding of these probabilities through gradual replacements. The upper bound uses a weighted directed graph whose vertices arrive in groups of decreasing sizes.

Motivated by emerging applications such as online marketplaces and quantum switches, we study a dynamic bipartite matching model with impatient agents, where the two sides represent customers and suppliers. Agents of each type arrive according to an independent Poisson process, and the platform decides which pairs of agents to match. The agents are possibly impatient and may leave the system if not matched before their patience expires. The platform aims to maximize throughput, i.e., the number of matches per unit time. In this paper, we reveal an interesting phase transition in the computational hardness of throughput maximization. In particular, we show that approximating the optimal long-run throughput within a sufficiently small fixed relative error is NP-hard, even when all agents have rate-one exponential patience. This result implies a computational barrier to constructing near-optimal, efficiently executable matching policies that induce a matching process with fast mixing. On the other hand, when all agents on at least one side have infinite patience, we provide a simple polynomial-time algorithm that maximizes the throughput.

Previously, the best known offline bound was optimal only for constant-size patterns [Berendsohn, Kozma, and Opler, STOC'24], and the best known online bound was superlinear [Chalermsook, Pettie, Yingchareonthawornchai, SODA'24] even for a constant-size pattern. As a corollary, our BST algorithm yields an optimal sorting algorithm for a pattern-avoiding sequence that supports online insertions. Previously, an optimal sorting algorithm was achieved using a mergesort-like approach [Opler, FOCS'24] in a batch setting. A key technique is to apply recursive split decomposition [Chalermsook, Chuzhoy, Saranurak, ToC'23] jointly in time and space, along with the Marcus-Tardos proof of the Stanley-Wilf conjecture. Applying this estimate to an optimal transport potential yields a sharp entropy factorization for every finite-entropy input. Linearization also gives the spectral-gap lower bound $(n+1)/n^2$.

For general metrics with $n\geq2$, fewer than $n$ edge-comparison queries suffice to achieve distortion at most $2\log_2^* n-1$, which is near-constant even for very large inputs.

This allows us to produce smoothed analysis guarantees in several previously open settings. These include new smoothed analysis guarantees for subspace clustering and certifying robust entanglement of subspaces, where prior work could only establish least singular value bounds for fully random instances or only show non-robust genericity guarantees.

It computes all distances in $O(n^{2.9929729})$ worst-case time, improving both the recent deterministic bound $O(n^{2.9997})$ and the Las Vegas expected-time bound $O(n^{2.993805})$. ♻ ☆ Light Edge Fault Tolerant Graph Spanners
Greg Bodwin, Michael Dinitz, Ama Koranteng, Lily Wang
There has recently been significant interest in fault tolerant spanners, which are spanners that still maintain their stretch guarantees after some nodes or edges fail. This work has culminated in an almost complete understanding of the three-way tradeoff between stretch, sparsity, and number of faults tolerated. However, despite some progress in metric settings, there have been no results to date on the tradeoff in general graphs between stretch, lightness, and number of faults tolerated. We initiate the study of light edge fault tolerant (EFT) graph spanners, obtaining the first such results. First, we observe that lightness can be unbounded if we use the traditional definition (normalizing by the MST). We then argue that a natural definition of fault-tolerant lightness is to instead normalize by a min-weight fault tolerant connectivity preserver; essentially, a fault-tolerant version of the MST. However, even with this, we show that it is still not generally possible to construct $f$-EFT spanners whose weight compares reasonably to the weight of a min-weight $f$-EFT connectivity preserver. In light of this lower bound, it is natural to then consider bicriteria notions of lightness, where we compare the weight of an $f$-EFT spanner to a min-weight $(f' > f)$-EFT connectivity preserver. The most interesting question is to determine the minimum value of $f'$ that allows for reasonable lightness upper bounds. Our main result is a precise answer to this question: $f' = 2f$. In particular, we show that the lightness can be untenably large (roughly $n/k$ for a $k$-spanner) if one normalizes by the min-weight $(2f-1)$-EFT connectivity preserver. But if one normalizes by the min-weight $2f$-EFT connectivity preserver, then we show that the lightness is bounded by just $O(f^{1/2})$ times the non-fault tolerant lightness (roughly $n^{1/k}$, for a $(1+ε)(2k-1)$-spanner).

♻ ☆ Asymmetric graph alignment and the phase transition for asymmetric tree correlation testing

While substantial progress has been made in aligning correlated Erdős-Rényi graphs under symmetric settings, real-world networks often exhibit asymmetry in both node numbers and edge densities. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for asymmetric correlated Erdős-Rényi graphs, generalizing existing models to account for these asymmetries. We conduct a rigorous theoretical analysis of graph alignment in the sparse regime, where local neighborhoods exhibit tree-like structures. Our approach leverages tree correlation testing as the central tool in our polynomial-time algorithm, MPAlign, which achieves one-sided partial alignment under certain conditions. A key contribution of our work is characterizing these conditions under which asymmetric tree correlation testing is feasible: If two correlated graphs $G$ and $G'$ have average degrees $λs$ and $λs'$ respectively, where $λ$ is their common density and $s,s'$ are marginal correlation parameters, their tree neighborhoods can be aligned if $ss' > α$, where $α$ denotes Otter's constant and $λ$ is supposed large enough. The feasibility of this tree comparison problem undergoes a sharp phase transition since $ss' \leq α$ implies its impossibility. These new results on tree correlation testing allow us to solve a class of random subgraph isomorphism problems, resolving an open problem in the field.

Such groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and in all 59 benchmark instances. Given the coefficients of constructed models with up to 16 families, one language model names a true group first in 249 of 252 answers. On the benchmark instances, decompositions chosen by language models from the text solve faster than those of GCG's detector.

☆ CiGS: Conduction in Gaussian Splats for Interior Temperature Field from Thermal Images
Liu Zhenyuan, Bharath Seshadri, Bailey Miller, George Kopanas, Ionnais Gkioulekas, Bernd Bickel
We present a method for inferring the interior temperature distribution of a solid object from registered multi-view visible-spectrum and thermal images, even when the thermal views cover only part of its surface. We formulate steady-state heat conduction as a Laplace boundary value problem and solve it with a direct boundary integral equation discretized over a point cloud: a Gaussian reconstruction of the visible-spectrum images supplies the boundary geometry, and the thermal images supply the boundary data. We do not build surface or volume meshes at any stage in our method. Instead, we sample collocation points from rendered depth without the pixels at depth discontinuities, and use a density subtraction that keeps the interior evaluation accurate up to the surface. The whole chain is differentiable, and we use it to recover the pose and depth of heating pipes, insulation defects, and the shape of cracks from thermal images. We validate our method through experiments on boundary value problems with Dirichlet-only and mixed Dirichlet and Robin boundaries, using synthetic and real captured data on scenes with challenging topology. These experiments show that our method matches analytical solutions and has better accuracy than FEM solvers.

☆ From XR Sketches to CAD: Preserving Design Intent with AI
Trudi Di Qi
Extended reality (XR) allows designers to sketch shapes directly in 3D, but converting these sketches into editable, feature-based CAD requires interpreting their intent. A sketch may contain drawing errors, intended features, and design choices that remain open. Correcting every irregularity risks erasing intended features, while automatic completion may impose choices the designer has not made. We argue that AI should add precision without overriding design intent, considering both the resulting shape and how the CAD model behaves during later edits. To guide this process, we propose a conceptual framework that distinguishes errors from intentions in individual sketch properties and relates them to correction, preservation, and exploration in editable CAD. We also outline five research directions for sketch interpretation, CAD construction, and evaluation, with testable hypotheses for selected questions.

Heimdall, a learned controller, calls slow on 52% of an SSD's reads when 30% are slow. Uncertainty estimators, the remedy prescribed for its wrong guesses, cannot find them: nine of them do no better than a coin. The drive can. On one trace, 2% of the reads of 4 to 8 KiB that found less than 4 KiB outstanding while the drive was answering came back slow, and Heimdall called 96% of them slow. A 4,096-entry table of how the drive's recent reads came back, untrained and 21 ns a decision, ranks the wrong guesses at a median AUROC of 0.68 on 57 held-out traces, where the nine sit at 0.46 to 0.52, and it predicts slow reads better than Heimdall itself.

We curate a new benchmark suite for system-level proof generation, VeruSAGE-Bench, which consists of 849 proof tasks extracted from eight open-source Verus-verified Rust systems, covering operating systems, storage systems, memory allocators, and more. These tasks are much more complicated than those in previous benchmarks, containing on average more than 20x the formal specification (in Lines of Code) and requiring a much broader array of verification techniques. We evaluate six LLMs on VeruSAGE-Bench (o4-mini, GPT-5, Sonnet 4, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, Qwen3.5), and demonstrate that different models and agentic setups lead to vastly different success rates and costs. We also show that the best models possess impressive capability in writing correctness proofs and hence should inspire new ways of developing trustworthy software. Meanwhile, some difficult tasks in VeruSAGE-Bench stress even the best model, forcing long reasoning time (over an hour on the hardest tasks, 15.3 min per task on average), high token cost (USD 13.65 per task on average), and proof failures, which we hope will guide future improvements in models and agents. This is particularly true for a harder no-lemma version of VeruSAGE-Bench, where the helper lemmas written by human experts are removed: there, the best model proves only 41% of the tasks from the hardest project, at USD 96 per task.

♻ ☆ NemoANN: I/O-Efficient Filtered Vector Search on SSDs with Graph Tunneling SoCC'26

We introduce NemoANN, an I/O-efficient SSD-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) system for filtered search. Existing SSD-based systems either waste I/O on post-filtering or require expensive filter-aware index rebuilds. Our key insight is that a nonmatching node can never be a result, so the search needs only its small neighbor list, not the full-precision vector on SSD. NemoANN therefore checks each predicate before the SSD read and tunnels through non-matching nodes using in-memory routing metadata, preserving graph connectivity without modifying the index. On a 100M-vector benchmark, NemoANN reduces SSD reads by about 10x and improves throughput by 8.0x over post-filtering and by 5.0x over PipeANN-Filter, a state-of-the-art filtered SSD system, at 10% selectivity and 90% recall. The gains over post-filtering grow at lower selectivity, reaching 13.1x at 5% selectivity.

The greedy randomized adaptive search procedure (GRASP)-based approach provides substantial acceleration, but it does not guarantee yield optimality. Both approaches use a preprocessing pipeline to reduce the problem size. Experimental results on industrial designs demonstrate that, as expected, the ILP-based approach achieves superior solution quality. The GRASP-based approach leads to lower runtimes while still achieving solution quality that is comparable to the ILP-based solution. Together, these methods provide a trade-off between solution quality and efficiency for practical chiplet assembly optimization.
☆ Rethinking KV Caching for LLM Decode: Free-Space Optical KV Regeneration for Reduction of Memory Traffic

Long-context large language model (LLM) decoding repeatedly reads the historical key-value (KV) cache, making multi-head attention (MHA) memory-bandwidth-bound. Caching layer-input activations instead halves historical-cache storage and traffic, but requires regenerating KV from each cached activation. On digital accelerators such as GPUs, this regeneration takes far longer than fetching the activation from HBM. The KV regeneration overhead outweighs the savings from reduced memory traffic, shifting decode attention from a memory bottleneck to a compute bottleneck. We present OptiDecode, a hybrid optoelectronic decode-attention accelerator that regenerates historical KV using free-space optics and computes attention digitally. Projection weights remain resident on optical tiles, exploiting reuse across historical tokens for high-throughput optical regeneration. Scaling to large models introduces two challenges. First, distributing weights across tiles requires sending the same activations to every head group, while each readout die produces only partial KV. Activation replay shares one set of electrical-to-optical converters across head groups without costly broadcast. In-situ attention avoids transferring partial KV from readout dies to reducers by computing on them locally and exchanging only partial scores, probabilities, and partial outputs. Second, processing an activation chunk through all dependent stages takes longer than one activation-fetch interval. Chunk pipelining overlaps successive chunks so that OptiDecode sustains the HBM activation-fetch rate. OptiDecode demonstrates 1.92-1.99x decode-attention speedup over an ideal GPU KV-read baseline at equal peak HBM bandwidth (A100-B200), for 32K-token contexts across evaluated 30B-175B MHA models, approaching the 2x upper bound from halving historical memory traffic.

Existing edge-intelligence solutions predominantly address these dimensions in isolation, making it difficult to determine whether an observed degradation originates from sensor malfunction, data-distribution shift, malicious execution, hardware faults, or resource and thermal stress. This paper presents a causal cross-layer self-healing Edge-AI framework that continuously observes synchronized telemetry spanning sensor health, inference uncertainty, processor hardware-performance counters, accelerator and memory activity, power and thermal state, and communication conditions. A temporally informed causal reasoning engine estimates the most probable origin of abnormal behavior and quantifies diagnostic uncertainty, including under concurrent perturbations.

☆ A predictive, per-engine energy roofline of the Apple Neural Engine

The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) is in over a billion devices, but is characterized indirectly via CoreML. Using a CoreML-free fused-graph dispatch path, we measure the ANE, along with the Apple GPU and CPU on the same device, with per-engine energy accounting. The consumer-available roofline does not predict the ANE in practice. A critical correction is that the ANE sees two effective memory bandwidths: a slow activation path and a fast weight-stream path. Two roofline ridges follow, and the weight-stream ridge is below that of the GPU. The ANE single-operand compute peak decreases instead of plateauing. Its weight stream is byte-bound in fp16 but limited by the dequantizer's element rate in int8. As a result, int8 compression saves energy at unchanged throughput and an int4 lookup-table stream raises throughput and efficiency at a cost of 2.55 points of ImageNet top-1. The corrected roofline identifies the lower-energy ANE paths and bounds it from below. A constructed device map reproduces across four unique ANE generations. Results show that operators should be placed by arithmetic intensity and fused for optimal performance.

☆ Executable Archaeology: Reanimating the Logic Theorist
David Moews, Jeff Shrager
The Logic Theorist (LT), created by Allen Newell, J. C. Shaw, and Herbert Simon in 1955--1956, is regarded by some as the first artificial intelligence program. It was originally simulated by hand and written in a pseudocode called the Logic Language (LL), which was later called Information Processing Language One (IPL-I). LT was revised many times. The first machine-executed version was written in IPL-II and ran on the JOHNNIAC, and a late version was published in 1963 by Einar Stefferud as a pedagogical document and written in IPL-V, the only version of IPL that was formally released to the public. We describe a reanimation of both the IPL-I (LL) version of LT and the 1963 IPL-V version. Comparing the two reanimations illuminates the process of the invention of early AI algorithms and computer languages.

☆ A Nonlinear Abstract Domain for Bayesian Neural Networks
Qiuhan Gu, Gagandeep Singh
Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) explicitly model epistemic uncertainty by leveraging probability distributions over network parameters, making them better suited for risk-aware decision-making. Yet soundly propagating uncertainty through the network and capturing the entire output distribution to support predictive uncertainty quantification remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches are either sampling-based, providing no formal guarantees, or propagate only selected statistical properties, such as expectations and entropy, limiting their applicability to general probabilistic queries. To address these challenges, we present the first nonlinear abstract domain for soundly approximating complete probability distributions of BNNs. The abstract domain builds upon a novel marginal collecting concrete semantics that soundly abstracts the classical joint-measure semantics. It combines support partitioning with exponential-affine bounds to represent probability measures, capturing both discrete and continuous components of mixed distributions as well as nonlinear density shapes over bounded and unbounded supports. We develop sound abstract transformers that can efficiently handle high-dimensional affine transformations and nonlinear ReLU activations, while remaining highly parallelizable. We further extend the framework beyond BNNs to support bounded-loop probabilistic programs with Bayesian inference to demonstrate its generality. We implement the resulting abstract interpreter as a GPU-accelerated analyzer. Experimental results show that the framework significantly improves precision over existing probabilistic reasoning approaches while soundly capturing the complete output distribution, demonstrating strong efficiency and scalability.
☆ Decoupling Data Layouts from Algebraic Data Types
Christophe Gyurgyik, Alexander J Root, Benjamin Driscoll, Gabriel Radanne, Fredrik Kjolstad, Clément Pit-Claudel
Algebraic data types (ADTs) decouple the logical structure of data from physical layout choices that affect performance. For example, packing small fields into a word improves spatial locality, while storing co-accessed fields contiguously can enable vectorization. Such choices reinforce or undermine one another, with ramifications for compiler optimizations and memory management. Their interplay creates a combinatorial space of layouts with different runtime costs and memory footprints. The most favorable layout depends on the program's construction and destruction patterns, the characteristics of input data, and the target machine. Exploring this space requires control over layout decisions and a way to compose them while preserving program semantics. We provide both through rewrite rules over layouts, independent of any particular source language or bit-level encoding. Starting from a canonical layout derived from the ADT, these rules transform its representation while leaving the source program intact. We identify a local refinement criterion for proving each rewrite rule correct, so that layouts continue to represent every value and keep distinct values apart. Adding a new rule therefore only requires a proof satisfying this local criterion. We realize these rules in Isomer, a new pure functional programming language whose compiler specializes construction, pattern matching, and memory management to the chosen layouts. Using a default layout for all ADTs, Isomer achieves competitive performance against established functional compilers that automatically select layouts. Our rewrites further improve performance by tailoring layouts to each workload, permitting representations that prior work cannot attain or can only achieve through explicit changes to the source code.
♻ ☆ On Higher-Order Reachability Games vs May Reachability
Kazuyuki Asada, Hiroyuki Katsura, Naoki Kobayashi
We consider the reachability problem for higher-order functional programs and study the relationship between reachability games (i.e., the reachability problem for programs with angelic and demonic nondeterminism) and may-reachability (i.e., the reachability problem for programs with only angelic nondeterminism). We show that reachability games for order-n programs can be reduced to may-reachability for order-(n+1) programs, and vice versa. We formalize the reductions by using higher-order fixpoint logic and prove their correctness. We also discuss applications of the reductions to higher-order program verification.
♻ ☆ ETAS: An Effect-Typed Language for Agent Systems
Huiri Tan, Yikun Wang, Puyang Zhang, Shangyu Li, Jiasi Shen
Agent systems are programs that coordinate language-model queries, tool calls, human approvals, and ordinary computation, yet existing frameworks wire them together as opaque library objects outside compiler analysis. Treating agent systems from a programming-language perspective, we present Etas, an effect-typed language that elevates agents, tools, workflows, and behavioral specifications to first-class, compiler-checked constructs. Crucially, Etas separates escaping effects from persistent effect request summaries: handlers change how an operation is interpreted without erasing its effect request from the summary, while trace specs constrain permitted effect requests and their order. The compiler composes effect request summaries across calls and handlers, discharging satisfied trace specs statically and keeping a residual monitor where dynamic paths remain uncertain. We formalize Core Etas with terminal handlers, a trace-spec monitor construction, and an abstract analysis over monitor states, proving preservation, progress, effect coverage, and trace-spec safety. We implement a compiler, an optimizer, and a checked interpreter using Rust. Across compiler fixtures and coding-agent scenarios written in Etas, Etas successfully enforces callable bounds, effect operation ordering, and handled effect request visibility with zero mismatches. The compiler also implements agent-specific optimizations that reduce execution time by 23.2%. Across 12 Etas workflows, the combined token optimization passes reduce input tokens by 67.8% on paired-correct executions. First-class agent abstractions also enable recursive self-evolution for Etas programs. Across five harness evolution iterations, task accuracy rises from 69.9% to 78.9%.

☆ Associahedra are 8-colourable
David R Wood
Determining the chromatic number of associahedra is a long-standing open problem. Tan [arXiv:2611.05323] recently proved that associahedra are 12-colourable, which is the first constant upper bound. This paper adapts Tan's argument to show that associahedra are 8-colourable.
☆ Computing Independent Sets of Size Three in Disk Graphs
Anastasiia Tkachenko, Haitao Wang
We study the problem of computing an independent set of size three in disk graphs, where vertices correspond to disks in the plane and two vertices are adjacent if their disks intersect. While computing a maximum independent set in disk graphs is NP-hard, the fixed-size case admits more efficient solutions. Given a set of $n$ disks, we present an algorithm to compute an independent set of size three in the disk graph and our algorithm runs in randomized expected $O^*(n^{5/3})$ time, where $O^*$ hides a factor of $n^ε$ for an arbitrarily small $ε> 0$. Our approach introduces a framework based on semi-algebraic range searching and tree-structured biclique partitions, which allows us to group pairs of disjoint disks into canonical subsets and avoid redundant computations. When the centers of the disks are in convex position, we solve the problem in $O(n \log^2 n)$ deterministic time. We also consider the case in which the disks themselves are in convex position, i.e., each disk contributes to the boundary of the convex hull of all disks, and obtain an $O(n \log^2 n)$ time algorithm for this setting as well. Our techniques for these cases are based on geometric properties of disk arrangements. In particular, they rely on new structural lemmas that reduce the problem to efficiently testing certain ordered configurations of disks. Our results improve upon the straightforward quadratic time approach and demonstrate how geometric structures and range searching techniques can be leveraged to solve fixed-size independent set problems in disk graphs more efficiently. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of independent sets of size three in disk graphs. Our results show that even this smallest nontrivial case exhibits rich structural properties, especially under convexity assumptions.

☆ Tight Bounds for Differentially Private Cut Release
Chenghua Liu, Boning Meng
We give a polynomial-time algorithm for releasing a nonnegative weighted synthetic graph under $(\varepsilon,δ)$-edge differential privacy. Given an $n$-vertex nonnegative weighted graph $G=(V,w_G)$, the output $H=(V,w_H)$ satisfies, with probability at least $1-β$, simultaneously for every $S\subseteq V$, $|w_G(S,V\setminus S)-w_H(S,V\setminus S)| \leγw_G(S,V\setminus S)+O\bigl((n\log n)/(\varepsilonγ)\bigr)$, provided that $γ,\varepsilon,δ,β$ are at least inverse polynomial in $n$. For constant $γ,\varepsilon$ and $δ=β=n^{-10}$, this improves the recently obtained additive error bound of $O(n\log^7 n)$ to $O(n\log n)$. We also prove a matching $Ω(n\log n)$ lower bound. Our algorithm combines degree decomposition with private multiplicative weights, using a degree-sensitive semidefinite oracle to generate update proposals from single Gaussian samples. Each proposal is validated by a noisy check of its exact entropy decrease, and a joint Rényi analysis of sampling and validation avoids additional logarithmic losses.

☆ Cogirth-Strength Ratios and Matroid Rank Reduction
Yu Cong, Chao Xu, Yajie Zhao
In the rank-$p$ reduction problem, we are given a matroid with nonnegative element weights and seek a minimum-weight set of elements whose deletion lowers the rank by at least $p$. For graphic matroids, this is the minimum $(p+1)$-cut problem. Chekuri, Quanrud, and Xu developed a tree-packing algorithm for minimum $k$-cut, which relies on the fact that the minimum cut of a graph is at most twice its strength, the value of a maximum fractional packing of spanning trees. We generalize this approach from graphs to matroids. The matroid analogue of the minimum cut is the cogirth, the minimum weight of a cocircuit, and the analogue of graph strength is matroid strength, the value of a maximum fractional packing of bases. We show that if every matroid in a deletion-closed class has cogirth at most $d$ times its strength, then for every $p$, the natural linear programming relaxation of rank-$p$ reduction is within a factor of $d$ of the optimum. As a result, repeatedly deleting a minimum-weight cocircuit gives a $d$-approximation, and an optimal solution can be found deterministically in $n^{(2d-1)p+O(1)}$ time on $n$ elements. For graphs, $d=2$ and our framework specializes to the tree-packing approach. As applications, we bound the cogirth-strength ratio for two broad classes, and both bounds are tight. For quasi-graphic matroids, which include graphic, bicircular, frame, and lifted-graphic matroids, the ratio is at most $2$ for all weights, giving a $2$-approximation and an exact $n^{3p+O(1)}$-time algorithm. For $(k,\ell)$-count matroids of hypergraphs with $0\le \ell\le k$ and edge size at most $s$, the ratio is at most $ks$ under unit weights. This gives a $ks$-approximation and an exact $n^{(2ks-1)p+O(1)}$-time algorithm for unweighted rank-$p$ reduction.
☆ Important Cuts with Logical Constraints: A Meta-Theorem for Eulerian Digraphs
Václav Blažej, Satyabrata Jana, Jędrzej Olkowski, M. S. Ramanujan, Peter Strulo
Important separators are a standard tool in parameterized cut algorithms. An $S$-$T$ separator is important if it is inclusion-wise minimal and no separator of at most the same size leaves a strict superset of the vertices reachable from $S$ after deletion. Their use relies on a boundedness theorem: for fixed $k$, the number of important $S$-$T$ separators of size at most $k$ is at most a constant ($4^k$ to be precise) independent of the input size, even in directed graphs, and they can be enumerated efficiently. The classical theory, however, controls only the size of the separator, not the structure of the source side cut off by it. Once the source side is required to satisfy a condition such as acyclicity, bipartiteness, or another logical property, the corresponding maximal source sides can be unbounded in general digraphs. This obstruction is fundamentally related to hardness phenomena in directed deletion problems such as Directed Odd Cycle Transversal}. Prior to this work, even in undirected graphs, boundedness of such maximal constrained source sides was known only in more specialized settings, not at the level of generality considered in our work.

☆ Matroid Parity Meets Vertex Splitting
Hitendra Kumar, Pritesh Kumar, Madhumita Kundu, Saket Saurabh
A vertex split replaces a vertex by two non-adjacent descendants and partitions its incident edges between them. We study exclusive $\ell$-shallow splitting, where each original vertex has at most $\ell+1$ descendants, with the aim of obtaining a forest, a pseudoforest, or a cluster graph. We consider two natural objectives: minimizing the total number of split operations and minimizing the number of original vertices that are split. Our main conceptual contribution is a connection between vertex splitting and matroid parity. For both forests and pseudoforests, we give a characterization of feasible splitting sequences that leads, via weighted linear matroid parity, to polynomial-time algorithms for minimizing the number of split vertices when $\ell=2$. These algorithms are complemented by NP-hardness for every fixed $\ell\ge3$; for pseudoforests, hardness holds even on graphs of maximum degree four. The total number of split operations behaves differently: for both sparse target classes, this objective is polynomial-time solvable for every $\ell$, using matroid intersection. For cluster graphs, both objectives admit linear-time algorithms when $\ell=1$ and are NP-hard for every fixed $\ell\ge2$. Together, these results identify how the target class, the local splitting bound, and the choice of objective determine the complexity of vertex splitting.

♻ ☆ Online Drone Coverage of Targets on a Line
Stefan Dobrev, Konstantinos Georgiou, Evangelos Kranakis, Danny Krizanc, Lata Narayanan, Jaroslav Opatrny, Denis Pankratov, Sunil Shende
We study the online target coverage problem for a mobile drone equipped with a camera with fixed scanning half-angle $α\in (0, π/2)$. Targets appear online at arbitrary positions along the $x$-axis, and upon each arrival the drone must move to a feasible position whose visibility interval covers both the newly revealed target and all previously arrived targets. The objective is to minimize the total Euclidean length of the drone's trajectory, evaluated against an optimal offline trajectory via the competitive ratio. We establish exact competitive ratios across the range $α\in (0, π/2)$ for three natural baseline algorithms,\textsc{Straight-Up}, \textsc{Cone-Apex}, and \textsc{Greedy}. We then analyze fixed-angle steering strategies and derive the optimal fixed-angle algorithm $β^*$-\textsc{Hedge}, which improves upon the baselines for $α\in (π/6, π/3)$ and peaks at $5/4$ when $α= π/4$. Going further, we introduce a family of memoryless, state-based linear interpolation algorithms $\mathcal{A}_λ$ (generalizing the \textsc{Midpoint} rule at $α= π/4$) and prove that the optimized algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{λ^*}$ strictly outperforms $β^*$-\textsc{Hedge} throughout $α\in (0, π/3)$, achieving a tight competitive ratio of $\sqrt{3/2} \approx 1.2247$ at $α= π/4$ while matching the optimal bound $\cscα$ for $β^*$-\textsc{Hedge} on $[π/3, π/2)$. Finally, we establish a universal lower bound on the competitive ratio of any deterministic or randomized online algorithm (against an oblivious adversary) across the entire domain $α\in (0, π/2)$. This lower bound attains its maximum at $α= π/4$ with value $(1 + \sqrt{2})/2 \approx 1.2071$, narrowing the optimal competitive ratio at $α= π/4$ to the interval $[(1+\sqrt{2})/2,\, \sqrt{3/2}]$.

♻ ☆ 3SUM Made Simpler (Without Matrix Multiplication), $k$-SUM Hypothesis Refuted for Odd $k$, and Real 3SUM/APSP Derandomized
Timothy M. Chan, Reina Itakura, Zhiyuan Ma, Yuancheng Yu
Recently, a truly subquadratic algorithm for the 3SUM problem and a truly subcubic algorithm for the all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) problem were found by Anthropic, as reported by Alman and Vassilevska Williams (2026). These algorithms relied on a new subroutine for rectangular matrix multiplication with selected output entries, which was obtained by modifying known matrix multiplication techniques of Schönhage (1981) and Coppersmith (1982). 1. We present a different truly subquadratic randomized algorithm for 3SUM for integer inputs. It completely avoids the use of matrix multiplication but instead modifies known dynamic programming algorithms for subset convolution and the zeta transform, which rely only on simple subtraction tricks via inclusion--exclusion (and does not even require fast Fourier transform), and so is conceptually easier to understand (the whole solution is about 5 pages long). 2. Following a similar approach, we obtain a randomized algorithm for $k$-SUM for integer inputs for odd constant $k$ in $O(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil-\varepsilon_k})$ time for some constant $\varepsilon_k>0$, disproving the $k$-SUM Hypothesis for all odd $k$. 3. Existing reductions from 3SUM and APSP to selected-entries rectangular matrix multiplication were randomized in the case of real-valued input. We present new deterministic reductions, yielding a truly subquadratic deterministic algorithm for Real 3SUM and a truly subcubic deterministic algorithm for Real APSP.
