♻ ☆ Fine-Grained Complexity of Approximating Vector Knapsack: A Faster Algorithm and Equivalence with $k$-SUM in 2D
Karl Bringmann, Ariel Kulik, Karol Węgrzycki
We revisit the $d$-dimensional Vector Knapsack problem (abbreviated as $d$-Knapsack): Given a $d$-dimensional capacity vector and a set of items, each with a $d$-dimensional weight vector and a profit, the goal is to select a set of items that maximizes the total profit without exceeding the capacity in any dimension. For any $d \ge 2$, the best known approximation scheme for $d$-Knapsack runs in time $O(n^{\lceil d/\varepsilon \rceil - d})$ [Caprara, Kellerer, Pferschy, Pisinger '00]. We improve this running time to $n^{\frac{d-1}{2\varepsilon} + O(d)}$. This is the first improvement for $d$-Knapsack in over 25 years, and the first result that improves the exponent by a constant factor, as all prior algorithms had an exponent of $d/\varepsilon \pm O(d)$. We achieve this speedup by designing the first meet-in-the-middle algorithm for $d$-Knapsack. This requires replacing the LP solver used in prior algorithms by a dynamic programming algorithm to generate representative solutions, building on an LP-based structural argument. We further establish a fine-grained equivalence of 2-Knapsack and $k$-SUM: For $k = \lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil - 1$, computing a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation for 2-Knapsack has the same time complexity as the $k$-SUM problem up to a factor $n^{O(1)}$, where the $O(1)$ is independent of $\varepsilon$. Consequently, unless $k$-SUM admits substantially faster algorithms than are currently known, 2-Knapsack requires time $n^{\frac 1{2\varepsilon} - O(1)}$, which together with our algorithm establishes the optimal running time exponent of 2-Knapsack as $\frac 1{2\varepsilon} \pm O(1)$. Conversely, if significantly faster algorithms for $k$-SUM are found, they automatically transfer to 2-Knapsack.

♻ ☆ Pauli-Z Moment Matrices in the Variational Quantum Power Method: Goemans-Williamson Rounding, Qubit Locking, and a Correlation-Based Circuit-Cutting Heuristic
Ammar Daskin
The matrix of single- and two-qubit Pauli-Z expectation values of any quantum state is the moment matrix of its computational-basis outcome distribution; it therefore lies in the cut polytope and, in particular, is a feasible point of the degree-2 Sum-of-Squares (Goemans-Williamson, GW) relaxation. Applying GW random-hyperplane rounding to this matrix yields cuts of expected weight at least alpha_GW times the state's energy. This observation and the resulting bound are not new: the bound is the GW inequality applied to the circuit's covariance matrix, and it was stated and used in exactly this form by Martinez, Fawzi and Stilck Franca, who interpret it as showing that a classical surrogate nearly reproduces the circuit and add noisy-circuit guarantees and hardware experiments; relax-and-round of QAOA correlation matrices, with spectral rather than hyperplane rounding, was introduced earlier by Dupont and Sundar. The bound is also not stronger than what direct computational-basis sampling of the state already gives in expectation. In this note we revisit the bound as a post-processing of the two-point data produced by variational algorithms such as QAOA and the Variational Quantum Power Method (VQPM), and give an energy-leakage bound for VQPM qubit locking. We further discuss a heuristic that uses the connected Z-correlation matrix to propose candidate qubit bipartitions for circuit cutting, in the spirit of existing correlation- and mutual-information-based partitioning methods, together with product-state error bounds in terms of quantum mutual information. Pairwise Z-correlations neither certify product structure of the state nor factorization of the underlying unitary, and the error bounds require quantities not available from Z-data alone.

♻ ☆ jXBW: A Compressed Index Enabling Structure-Aware JSONL Retrieval for Structured RAG
Yasuo Tabei
Providing structured information to large language models (LLMs) has been shown to improve multi-step reasoning and factual accuracy (e.g., StructRAG, ICLR 2025; RAS, ICLR 2026); recent retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems reconstruct structure from retrieved text on every query. When the corpus is already structured, as in JSON Lines (JSONL), used for LLM prompts, chemical compounds, and geospatial objects, this per-query rebuilding can be replaced by direct structural retrieval. Its core operation is substructure search: finding all JSON objects in a collection that contain a given query tree. Existing approaches index each object separately, so index space and query time grow with collection size; XML-based engines add conversion overhead and semantic mismatches. We propose jXBW, a compressed index for fast substructure search over JSONL, combining three innovations: (i) a merged tree representation that consolidates repeated structures across objects, (ii) a succinct tree encoding based on the eXtended Burrows-Wheeler Transform (XBW), and (iii) a three-phase substructure search algorithm on this encoding. Together they achieve query-dependent complexity in compressed space: the search avoids a full scan of the collection, and its cost grows with the numbers of candidate matches and results. Experiments on seven real-world datasets, including PubChem (1 million compounds) and OpenStreetMap (6.6 million objects), show that jXBW outperforms the strongest tree-based baseline by 16x on the smallest dataset and by up to 2,800x on the largest, while the XML-based engine Saxon does not complete the 1,000-query workload on PubChem within 24 hours. jXBW brings substructure search over million-object JSONL collections into the sub-millisecond range.

♻ ☆ Nonuniform Buy-at-Bulk Network Design: Improved Approximation and LP Integrality Gap
Iman Gholami, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi
In nonuniform buy-at-bulk network design, we are given an undirected graph and $h$ terminal pairs with positive demands, and we must route every demand at minimum total cost when each network resource has two independent parameters: a fixed buying price paid once if the resource is used, and a per-unit rental cost (or physical length) paid proportionally to the traffic it carries. Unlike the uniform-cost or single-sink variants, the general multicommodity problem allows unrelated buying and rental metrics across arbitrary source--sink pairs, arbitrary demands, and both edge and node resources. We give a deterministic polynomial-time $O(\log^2 h / (\log\log h)^2)$-approximation algorithm for undirected nonuniform buy-at-bulk network design. The guarantee holds for edge costs, node costs, and their combination, and applies to arbitrary positive rational demands with no dependence on the number of vertices or the numerical demand ratio. This improves upon the $O(\log^4 h)$ bound of Chekuri, Hajiaghayi, Kortsarz, and Salavatipour (2010) for unrestricted instances. Our result also establishes the same $O(\log^2 h / (\log\log h)^2)$ upper bound on the integrality gap of the natural affine multicommodity flow LP, bounding integral buying and rental costs separately against their fractional counterparts and preserving zero rental budgets exactly. We complement this with an $Ω(\log h/\log\log h)$ lower bound on the integrality gap of the natural LP that holds already for edge-only instances.
♻ ☆ Capacitated Line Aggregation with Maximum Delay
Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu
We study capacitated line aggregation with per-batch maximum delay. Requests arrive over time at locations on a rooted half-line and are served in instantaneous batches of at most $g$ requests. Each batch pays the distance to its farthest request plus the waiting time of its oldest request. The objective is to minimize the total cost. We give a deterministic online algorithm with competitive ratio $36+12\sqrt3$. The algorithm uses a Next Fit idea along paths of nested time intervals: it assigns a new group to an existing batch when a path-load test permits, and opens a new batch otherwise. The path load controls both capacity and the cost of opening new batches. Randomizing the common scale improves the expected competitive ratio to $(18+6\sqrt3)/\ln2$ against an oblivious adversary. Both guarantees extend to arbitrary indivisible request sizes. We also study capacitated LAD in the learning-augmented model. Advice revealed at its service times allows $(1+ε)$-consistency against every complete feasible advice schedule and $O(ε^{-2})$-robustness. The analysis charges repeated switches to successive decreases in the remaining advice cost. Controlled synthetic experiments with 9,180 exact-rational monitor runs illustrate both the benefit of optimal advice and the delayed fallback caused by the stated conservative constants. We provide all inputs, outcomes, and reproducibility code; the experiments do not claim performance on learned predictions or large-scale demand traces.

☆ GRASP: Query-Adaptive Graph Retrieval framework with Cross-Attention Scoring and Path Sufficiency Verification for Question Answering
Rui Xu, Le Wang, Tianyue Wang
Retrieval quality is a key factor in the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), particularly when retrieval is performed over structured knowledge graphs. Graph-based retrieval requires decisions about candidate-edge scoring, traversal termination, and the sufficiency of the retrieved evidence. We propose GRASP, a query-adaptive graph retrieval framework that jointly addresses these decisions during the retrieval process. A cross-attention scorer models fine-grained interactions between individual query tokens and candidate edges, providing query-specific signals for edge selection. A learned stopping gate conditions traversal termination on the query, traversal state, and hop depth, allowing the retrieval depth to adapt to the current retrieval state. A sufficiency classifier further evaluates the assembled path before generation and triggers re-retrieval when the evidence is predicted to be incomplete. We evaluate GRASP on three biomedical question-answering benchmarks with different graph scales and answer lengths, using biomedical question answering as a representative setting for evaluating graph-based RAG retrieval. GRASP consistently improves over the strongest learned baseline across the evaluated retrieval and generation metrics. The unsupported-claim rate is reduced by 8.9% to 13.2% across the three benchmarks, with the largest reduction on the benchmark with the longest generated answers. The retrieval gains are more pronounced under higher candidate density, while ablation results indicate that the three components provide complementary improvements.
☆ Prepare Lighter and Faster for Open-Vocabulary Queries: A Query-Wise 3D Segmenter for Gaussian Splatting WACV 2027
Nhat-Quynh Le-Pham, Khoi Nguyen, Binh-Son Hua
Open-vocabulary 3D understanding aims to localize and segment arbitrary objects beyond predefined categories. However, existing approaches based on Gaussian Splatting often rely on expensive preprocessing and lengthy training, limiting their applicability when fast and lightweight solutions are desired. We propose a lightweight, training-free framework for query-driven 3D instance segmentation on Gaussian Splatting. Instead of conventional mask-wise CLIP embeddings, we use dense pixel-level CLIP features to preserve fine-grained semantic information and enable flexible text-driven localization without relying on predefined instance proposals. Given a text query, we identify a high-quality target region in a carefully selected pivot view and propagate it across views using a video segmentor, providing consistent and comprehensive coverage of the target instance. We then lift the resulting 2D tracklets to 3D Gaussians through a novel visibility voting strategy, yielding accurate 3D segmentation masks with clean object boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups over existing open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of our framework for efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.

☆ ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
Matthias Jammot, Pembe Gizem Özdil
Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

♻ ☆ Vertigo Vertigo: Reconstructing a Cinematic Ideal through its Predictive AI Double SIGGRAPH
Adam Cole, Mick Grierson
Vertigo Vertigo is a scene-for-scene AI reconstruction of Hitchcock's Vertigo (1958), generated from only 2.78% of the original film's frames. Using this sparse set of keyframe anchors, we perform first-last frame interpolation via a large video diffusion model to predict the intervening sequences. Vertigo is itself a film about the obsessive reconstruction of an artificial ideal; Vertigo Vertigo extends this logic to the material of the film, treating the canonical text as a probe for the normative conventions of classical cinema encoded within generative systems. Evaluated through computational analysis and critical feedback from media theorists (Lev Manovich, Shane Denson, Kevin L. Ferguson), the artifact demonstrates remarkable structural fidelity: 73.1% of frames are recognizable as plausible renditions of Vertigo and only 3.6% fail catastrophically. This fidelity suggests that cinematic norms are deeply compressed within the model's latent priors. Aesthetically, the reconstruction is rendered as an unstable overlay between the original film and its predictive shadow, fueling a persistent doubt in the viewer's perception of authenticity -- a 21st-century vertigo. The work argues that generative media is not a paradigm shift from cinema but an acceleration of its logic of desire and false authenticity, extending from classical Hollywood through to the predictive media environments now reshaping contemporary perception.

Operating Systems 2
☆ TailGuard-GDS: Tail-Safe Control of GPU Storage Data Movement
Jiaqi Liu, Fan Yang, Xiaohang Shi, Xianzhe Zhang, Tao Jiang, Guojun Yuan, Zhan Wang, Guangming Tan
AI runtimes move state between NVMe storage and GPU memory on critical paths. GPUDirect Storage (GDS) removes host staging, yet our eight-H100 measurements show it is not consistently tail-optimal for semantically identical GPU-buffer operations. The preferred path varies with operation, request size, concurrency, placement, and resource contention; bandwidth and tail-latency winners can disagree. Frameworks specify what moves and when, while GPU I/O stacks expose mechanisms; neither combines phase semantics with measured tail behavior to choose a delivery plan. We present TailGuard-GDS, a runtime that selects a semantically equivalent plan per application phase. It profiles plans varying backend, request shape, and placement, minimizes GPU-visible tail latency under phase constraints, and revisits decisions as conditions change. Resource reuse keeps policy lookup and switching at microsecond-scale overhead. Integrated with PyTorch FSDP and DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, TailGuard reduces FSDP step p95 by 18.4% and GPU-idle p95 by 25.3% versus the strongest fixed path. Across five eight-GPU ZeRO-3 workloads, step p95 falls 7.9-24.6% versus fixed host staging and 28.4-42.6% versus fixed GDS. Against tuned DeepSpeed AIO, TailGuard reduces step p95 by 5.6% and raises estimated throughput by 6.1%.
comment: This is a full-length research article. The manuscript is 35 pages and contains 14 figures and 17 tables, including the appendix. It is not under consideration elsewhere
♻ ☆ DeltaBox: Millisecond-Scale Sandbox Checkpoint and Rollback for Stateful AI Agents ATC 2026
Yunpeng Dong, Jingkai He, Shiqi Liu, Yuze Hou, Dong Du, Zhonghu Xu, Si Yu, Baochuan Yang, Yubin Xia, Haibo Chen
Emerging LLM-powered AI agent workloads, such as test-time tree search and reinforcement learning (RL), require high-frequency state exploration, relying on rapid checkpoint/restore (C/R) of the complete sandbox state, including files and process state. Existing mechanisms duplicate the entire state, causing hundreds of milliseconds to seconds of latency per C/R, which severely bottlenecks deep search and large-scale fan-outs. We observe that consecutive sandbox states between checkpoints differ only marginally. Therefore, instead of full duplication, a sandbox should only duplicate the changes between consecutive checkpoints (Key Insight), yet the lack of OS support makes this hard to realize. We propose a new OS-level abstraction, DeltaState, that delivers change-based C/R for agents through co-designed OS mechanisms. First, DeltaFS checkpoints file state by freezing the writable layer and inserting a new one, turning updates into copy-on-write and rollback into a layer switch. Second, DeltaCR quickly restores process state by forking from a frozen template process. A coordinator pairs the two so each checkpoint is one consistent (filesystem, memory) state. Building on these mechanisms, we present DeltaBox, an agent sandbox with millisecond-level C/R. On SWE-bench, DeltaBox hides its checkpoint work (10.83 ms) under inference and rolls back in a mean 1.86 ms, with the same warm-template fork driving low-cost RL rollout fan-out. DeltaBox is open-sourced at https://github.com/delta-box.

Hardware Architecture 21
☆ WaferTetris: Efficient Freeform Mapping on Wafer-Scale Accelerators
Dayou Du, Congjie He, Andrew Boutros, Luo Mai, Vaughn Betz, Jianyi Cheng
Wafer-scale accelerators offer massive compute capacity through hundreds of thousands of processing elements (PEs) interconnected across a single wafer, but realizing this potential requires efficient application mapping. Their scale makes programming these systems and mapping applications onto them challenging. Existing approaches rely on template-based mappings to maintain productivity, but these templates restrict the mapping design space. In particular, they impose fixed geometric layouts over the PE grid, often leaving compute and memory resources underutilized. In this work, we present WaferTetris, a system that removes these geometric restrictions through freeform mapping. Its Tetris-like strategy flexibly packs computation across the wafer, improving PE utilization and usable memory capacity while preserving PE-task code. We develop a recurrence-based throughput model that captures branch-and-join dependencies to guide spatial parallelism, and an architecture model with per-color gates that enable existing FPGA place-and-route algorithms to enforce WSE routing constraints. We evaluate WaferTetris on Cerebras WSE-3 using LLM decoding and scientific stencil benchmarks. For LLM decoding, it achieves up to $4.42\times$ the system throughput of a template-based automatic mapping baseline on the same fabric size. Compared with the manually optimized WaferLLM, WaferTetris supports $1.8\times$ the context length for LLaMA3.1-8B (80k versus 44k), while delivering equal or higher per-user throughput at matched context lengths, up to $1.10\times$.
☆ EventSpikeSeg: Memory-Aware Mixed-Signal Architecture for Event-Camera Spiking Segmentation
Amir Mohammad Khadem Hosseini, Sattar Mirzakuchaki
Event-camera segmentation requires persistent neural state despite sparse input events, making memory organization a central constraint on embedded implementation. We present EventSpikeSeg, a mixed-signal architecture combining resident capacitor memory with shared analog processing in GF180MCU 180-nm CMOS. Its 25-population spiking encoder-decoder has 143,824 synaptic weights but requires 30,976,000 membrane states at 440 x 640 resolution. The mapping specifies chronological 5-ms model updates, digital event/address services and 64-state capacitor banks. Characterization covers 22 module families and 74 operating points, distinguishing transistor simulations from digital-library estimates. Nominal results include 41.711 microwatts biased neuron-core power, 3.338-pJ positive terminal energy for a 1.4-microsecond cell read, and 0.531-mV selected-state drift over a 5-ms extracted-tile hold. Commit and coupling errors are reported separately. The software checkpoint records 27.976% mean intersection-over-union on a held-out six-class DSEC split; this is not hardware accuracy. Component layouts and simulation evidence quantify local implementation costs and expose storage replication and service scheduling as scaling constraints. A detailed SPICE-calibrated behavioral forward simulation of one full-resolution DSEC frame achieves 24.26% mean intersection-over-union, versus 26.22% for the matched PyTorch reference, using a compact 5-fF bank variant and external count/voltage calibration. Physical full-network operation, system energy and mismatch robustness remain unverified.
☆ Mutable Inference: Architecting LLM Accelerators for Inference-Time Learning
Yimin Gao, Liangtao Dai, Melika Morsali, Junting Huo, Mircea Stan
Long-context LLMs must retain growing histories, but full attention makes each new token increasingly expensive. Inference-time learning (ITL) offers another approach. The model keeps training on the context during inference, retaining what it learns in its weights. Recent work shows that ITL can match full-context attention quality while attending only to a recent fixed-size window. This bounds attention costs but adds Learning (backward computation and weight updates) alongside Prediction (the forward pass) costs. Inference accelerators assume fixed weights, while training accelerators target complete training steps. This work identifies two opportunities. Attention's non-matrix operations leave enough idle matrix capacity for Learning, while selected layers can tolerate delayed weight updates with little quality loss. We exploit both with Learning While Serving (LWS), an inference accelerator architecture that shares compute hardware between latency-critical Prediction and deadline-flexible Learning. Hardware-managed per-layer weight versioning allows Learning to publish updates while in-flight computations read older versions. Resumable reduction blocks let Learning kernels span fragmented idle windows and yield to Prediction, while dedicated softmax-gradient units relieve vector contention. On modeled datacenter and edge NPUs, LWS hides Learning within Prediction, sustaining Prediction-only throughput while preserving 99.3% of fully fresh Learning's quality benefit for TTT-E2E 3B at 128K tokens. Across nine models, LWS achieves 1.6x the throughput of serial execution and 1.3x that of the best prior co-execution architecture. RTL synthesis shows that LWS adds 1.5% to NPU core area without another MAC array. By efficiently turning idle inference capacity into learning capacity, LWS establishes inference-time learning as a first-class workload for future LLM accelerators.
☆ OpenLayout: An Open and Agentic-Driven Platform for Holistic VLSI Physical Design and Benchmarking
Qiufeng Li, Sizhe Tang, Quan Cheng, Zirui Wang, Wantong Li, Tian Lan, Weidong Cao
Physical design automation of very large-scale integrated circuits (VLSI) has made significant strides, progressing from single-stage placement and routing toward increasingly integrated full-flow implementation. Yet, existing approaches struggle with the vast design space optimization (DSO) arising from diverse technology nodes, circuit designs, and varied constraints. The substantial runtime of physical-design tools further exacerbates this challenge, leaving industrial workflows heavily dependent on experienced engineers to navigate the design space and achieve power, performance, and area (PPA) targets, incurring significant engineering effort. We argue that large language models (LLMs) with strong reasoning capabilities, enriched with distilled human design expertise, offer a promising path toward efficient and automated DSO. Unlike traditional algorithms, LLMs can interpret complex design contexts and naturally incorporate human expertise expressed in natural language for reasoning, acting, observing, and adapting throughout the design process, a capability that conventional optimization methods cannot exploit. To this end, we present OpenLayout, an agentic platform that leverages multi-agent collaboration with embedded design knowledge to enable self-iterative DSO. We further introduce OpenLayout-Bench, a benchmark targeting advanced technology nodes with commercial EDA tools to systematically evaluate physical design automation capabilities of LLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that OpenLayout achieves state-of-the-art performance, with approximately 20% accuracy improvement over baseline methods. Our work is open-sourced at https://github.com/fenggev56/OpenLayout

☆ The State Is Not the Bottleneck: A Paged-State Gated-DeltaNet Tile on a Tri-Mode Multicast Mesh, Bit-Exact from RTL to Silicon
Cong Xu, Ravi Sankar
Linear-attention language models replace a growing key-value cache with a recurrent state of fixed size. On an edge FPGA, this state can exceed the on-chip memory and must be paged to external memory. This paper asks whether such paging dominates the cost of decoding (generating tokens). We built a hardware tile that computes one complete layer of a custom 369-million-parameter hybrid Gated DeltaNet model on an Agilex 5 FPGA and pages its recurrent state. The model state needs 6.2 MiB, whereas the device has 0.87 MiB of block memory. Paging adds 26.0 MB of memory traffic per decoded token, at most 11.2 percent of the calculated total. On the board at 75 MHz, with synthetic weights, one token takes 11.15 ms in this layer. The matrix-vector products with the weights take about 62 percent of this time and the state phase, including the paging, 13 percent. The tile is one node of a multicast mesh of tri-mode processing elements. We measure the error of the fixed-point arithmetic against floating point and check that the hardware agrees bit for bit with a fixed-point reference. In simulation, the state logic agrees with the reference on all 18 recurrent layers. On the board, six builds pass all 30 runs of 64 tokens and two runs of 1,024 tokens. For this model and memory interface, the delivery of the weights limits the decoding performance, and the recurrent state does not. State paging is therefore practical for such a model on an edge FPGA.

☆ The Transformer Paradigm: Dynamic Processing and a New Principle of Inference
Marco Giunti, Fabrizia Giulia Garavaglia
We argue that the Transformer revolution is not adequately understood as a merely quantitative expansion of deep learning, but as the emergence of a new paradigm based on a different principle of inference. We interpret the Transformer as a system in which token representations are transformed by parameterized transformations, or transforming concepts. During inference, some of these transformations are dynamically constructed from the current input: previously acquired transformations are first adapted and then applied. At the mechanical-structural level, this dynamic processing is realized through output-weight interconnections, whereby outputs of some networks determine the weights of others. The resulting mode of processing, which we call Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP), provides a framework for explaining strong prompt sensitivity and opens research directions concerning interpretability, control, alternative AI architectures, neuromorphic systems, and possible biological realizations of dynamic processing.

☆ DiffusionSSD: Achieving Extreme Visual Compression with Dual-stage Diffusion and Cross-level Near-Data Processing
Kuai Yu, Wen Li, Shengwen Liang, Jie Zhang, Ying Wang, Huawei Li, Xin Yao, Renhai Chen, Gong Zhang
Growing visual data overwhelms storage on resource-constrained edge devices, making compression essential. Traditional codecs offer inadequate rate-distortion performance, motivating the exploration of diffusion codecs. Diffusion codecs face two limitations: (1) At the algorithm level, diffusion decoders preserve perceptual quality under extreme compression, but require substantial computation. (2) At the architecture level, in NPU-centered devices, neural codecs occupy the NPU, interfering with other AI applications. Meanwhile, the complex codec pipeline incurs long I/O paths, leading to additional overhead and energy cost. To address these issues, we propose DiffusionSSD, a cross-level near-data processing framework for extreme visual data compression on edge devices, using an algorithm-architecture co-design method. Specifically, (1) at algorithm level, we present Dual-stage Diffusion, a lightweight solution tailored for diffusion codecs that employs patchification and single-step diffusion, reducing computation cost while preserving perceptual quality; (2) at architecture level, we introduce a Cross-level Near Data Processing architecture that integrates the proposed computational universal flash storage (cUFS) and LPDDR-PIM, enabling codecs to be entirely offloaded to data side while reducing visual-data movement and avoiding SoC redesign; (3) at system level, combining both the algorithm and the underlying architecture, we propose a Patch-Workload co-aware scheduling scheme to enable more efficient system-level execution. Experiments show that Dual-stage Diffusion maintains comparable perceptual quality while reducing computation cost by up to 92.7%. Compared with NPU+DRAM and near-data-processing design such as SmartSSD, cUFS+PIM improves coding throughput by 2.32 times and 2.91 times on average, respectively.

☆ SIMTurn: Lightweight Divergent Subgroup Scheduling for Intra-Warp Synchronization
Nikhil Rout, Joe Samuel Rosh, Blaise Tine
Stack-based reconvergence enables efficient SIMT execution with a shared warp program counter and compact control-flow state. However, its fixed serialization of divergent paths can deadlock programs that rely on intra-warp synchronization: a spinning subgroup may prevent a resource-holding sibling from executing. Independent Thread Scheduling (ITS) enables finer-grained progress through per-thread execution state, but introduces additional hardware cost. We present SIMTurn, a lightweight compiler-hardware mechanism that enables forward progress among divergent subgroups while retaining stack-based reconvergence. SIMTurn combines a compiler-inserted yield instruction at potentially blocking loops with a bounded pool of resumable subgroups. The scheduler allows a waiting subgroup to yield to a sibling that can make progress, without requiring independent program counters for every thread. We implement SIMTurn in the compiler, simulator, and RTL on the open-source Vortex GPGPU and evaluate it against baseline IPDOM and per-thread ITS schemes. Across the evaluated GPU thread configurations, SIMTurn introduces only 17-24% scheduler-area overhead relative to IPDOM, compared with 39-91% for ITS, and stays within 8% of IPDOM on workloads that never need cross-subgroup progress. On kernels with genuine cross-subgroup parallelism, SIMTurn tracks ITS closely and is up to 2.7x faster than a software-serialized IPDOM baseline.

☆ Elasticy: A Runtime-Reconfigurable Architecture for Dynamic Streams
Konstantin J Hossfeld, Nathan Sobotka, Gina Sohn, Tun-Yu Chang, Kunle Olukotun
Reconfigurable Dataflow Accelerators (RDAs) have demonstrated high performance and energy efficiency for dense, regular tensor applications. However, conventional RDAs with static configurations show dramatically reduced performance and efficiency on irregular tensor workloads with data-dependent, non-uniform, dynamic tensor shapes. We propose Elasticy, a dynamically reconfigurable dataflow accelerator that employs streaming and tile abstractions to minimize the overhead of dynamic support. By encoding dynamic shapes into streams using rank-variable expressions, Elasticy exploits data-dependent tensor shape dynamism to minimize off-chip data traffic and wasted compute cycles. Elasticy employs stream-embedded reconfiguration information to trigger fine-grained runtime scheduling decisions. Elasticy also introduces a novel distributed linked streaming memory (DLSM) that more effectively uses on-chip memory to minimize off-chip data traffic and support dynamically sized tensors. Both reconfiguration and shape dynamism incur minimal overhead in Elasticy: reconfiguration occurs infrequently at the granularity of a stream of tiles, while rank-variable expressions enable lightweight handling of dynamic dimensions. On a Llama 3-8B decode layer, Elasticy achieves 92.6% of its roofline performance, compared to 69.7% on an H100. On evaluated GEMMs, the DLSM reduces total off-chip traffic by up to 61.4% relative to the best evaluated cache configuration, with no additional burden of programmer-managed memory. Elasticy's distributed runtime scheduler overlaps dependent kernels, speeding up kernel pairs by up to 1.42x. Programs can also run in both space and time: each phase of a layer's graph is pipelined spatially, while phases fold onto the same fabric over time. Compared to a traditional spatial accelerator, Elasticy achieves a 6.34x-31.67x improved area delay product on full layers.

Md Omar Faruque, Jingang Jin, João Paulo C. de Lima, Shouzhi Fang, William C. Tegge, Peipei Zhou, Qinru Qiu, Alex K. Jones
Edge AI increasingly relies on specialized accelerators for low-latency inference under tight resource and energy constraints, yet their efficiency remains limited by data movement. Prior work, CHARM, mitigates this overhead by overlapping data movement with computation. We observe that in-memory computing can further supplement tensor processing as a parallel accelerator while eliminating certain data movements entirely. We present CHARMING, a heterogeneous edge AI architecture that uses accuracy- and quantization-aware partitioning to distribute and concurrently execute inference workloads across tensor processing and in-memory computation. CHARMING partitions attention heads between an AIE array and an in-DRAM compute unit, balancing execution according to model architecture, sequence length, and precision while selecting heads to minimize accuracy degradation. CHARMING also integrates quantization into the AIE projection stage to further reduce data movement. We validate CHARMING end-to-end in hardware on AMD Versal VCK5000 and Alveo U200 platforms and evaluate LLM and video-generation models across multiple precisions using measured hardware results and simulation of the latest in-memory compute hardware. CHARMING improves prefill performance by up to 23.6 percent and decode performance by up to 44 percent over AIE-only acceleration. With int4 x int4 fixed-point in-memory computation, CHARMING reduces per-layer energy by up to 7.6 percent and improves energy-delay product by up to 24.7 percent, while maintaining accuracy similar to a 32-bit floating-point baseline.
☆ uhd-rfsoc: Bringing Off-the-Shelf RFSoC Boards to Unmodified UHD Applications
Wei Cheng, Yiming Li, Junyao Zheng, Cheng-Bin Chen, Tingjun Chen
Next-generation wireless research relies on software-defined radios (SDRs) with more channels and larger bandwidth. The USRP family is one of the most widely used SDR platforms, and much of the wireless software ecosystem is built on top of the USRP hardware driver (UHD). However, each USRP model comes with a fixed channel count, bandwidth, and streaming capability. Off-the-shelf radio frequency system-on-chip (RFSoC) boards, on the other hand, integrate up to 16 analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) and 16 digital-to-analog converters (DACs) operating at several gigasamples per second (GS/s), but existing UHD applications cannot directly use them. We present uhd-rfsoc, an open-source FPGA design and host software stack that turns these boards, including the 16-channel ZCU216 and the RFSoC 4x2, into standard UHD devices without modifying UHD. Through standard UHD calls, applications can configure the carrier frequency, channel count, the per-channel I/Q sample rate, and the wire format. uhd-rfsoc combines timestamped, flow-controlled sample transport in the FPGA with data plane development kit (DPDK) packet processing and vectorized sample conversion on x86 and Arm hosts. The built bitstreams for a number of RFSoC board configurations with varying RF data converter rates, channel counts, I/Q sample rates, and wire formats all successfully pass UHD's built-in streaming benchmarks. We further demonstrate compatibility with unmodified GNU Radio flowgraphs, a custom GPU-accelerated transceiver digital signal processing pipeline, as well as the OCUDU and Duranta 5G radio access network stacks using both software and commodity user equipment.
☆ A Unified Device-Level Physical Framework for DRAM Read Disturbance
Zhaoqiang Bai, Haocong Luo, Xinhe Wang, Xujing Li, Yuelin Jiang, Xuelu Huang, Guilei Wang, Hao Meng, Ataberk Olgun, Ismail Emir Yuksel, F. Nisa Bostancı, Jikun Wang, Onur Mutlu
Read disturbance in dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) depends on both local device interactions and the electrical conditions imposed by shared array circuitry. Here, we combine DIMM-level characterization results, device measurements, and TCAD simulations to interpret RowHammer, RowPress, and ColumnDisturb within a unified device-level physical framework. We relate charge evolution at the floating storage node to three key mechanisms: trap-assisted electron migration (EM), capacitive coupling (CC), and sense-amplifier-mediated disturb (SAMD). EM is local and trap-sensitive, while CC weakens with wordline separation. SAMD extends disturbance through shared column circuitry by modifying unselected-cell leakage under rail-level bitline biases, a contribution supported by the approximately ninefold higher OFF-state leakage measured relative to retention-like conditions for a high-voltage storage state. These distinct spatial ranges account for localized RowHammer and RowPress failures and remote ColumnDisturb populations with abrupt changes at subarray boundaries. We further interpret prolonged RowPress activation as a transition from an initial RowHammer-like transient to sustained leakage driven mainly by SAMD under held wordline and bitline biases. Within this device-level framework, trap effectiveness and storage-state-dependent leakage provide an interpretation of previously puzzling failure signatures, including the earlier onset of 0-to-1 RowHammer failures despite the predominance of 1-to-0 failures at high hammer counts. The same framework explains the observed RowPress and ColumnDisturb polarities and the duration-dependent reversal of neighboring- and passing-wordline effectiveness. These results provide a physical basis for developing compact DRAM reliability models across access patterns and array configurations.
☆ NEMESIS2.0: LLM-Aided Netlist-Driven Performance Equation Modeling for Accelerated Analog Circuit Sizing
Subhadip Ghosh, Ramesh Harjani, Sachin S. Sapatnekar
This work presents NEMESIS2.0, an open-source LLM-aided framework that automatically derives equation-based performance models for analog circuits. The resulting equations provide fast, accurate surrogates for SPICE evaluation. To validate the method, equation-based models are developed for seven circuit test cases in a commercial 65nm CMOS technology, covering 15 metrics on five operational transconductance amplifier topologies, and six metrics on two dynamic comparator topologies. When tested on 1000 unseen variants of these seven designs, each corresponding to a different set of independently sampled transistor sizes, the accuracy is found to be within 5% of SPICE. To demonstrate use cases for NEMESIS2.0, the generated models are used as performance evaluators in multiple transistor sizers based on different population-based stochastic search optimizers. For each of the seven test cases, transistor sizing is performed for 100 different sets of performance specifications, with final SPICE simulation confirming that 83.3% of the resulting designs meet all specifications after a single sizing run. The rest fail to meet the specifications due to discrepancies between the model and SPICE, and require iterative resizing under tightened specifications; all such scenarios meet specifications within five iterations. Within the transistor sizers, this equation-based performance analysis evaluates ~400 design candidates per second, versus 0.14 candidates per second for SPICE-based evaluation, achieving 196-238x sizing runtime speedup, including final SPICE verification.

☆ Lasso: Towards Sustainable AI-Generated Media Detection with Intel QAT On-Chip Compression
Darsh Asher, Joshua Kalyanapu, Kaushal Mhapsekar, Bita Aslrousta, Amna Hassan, Debayan Sengupta, Samira Mirbagher Ajorpaz
Synthetic text, images, and video are rising. Software-only detectors are power-hungry, too slow, and costly, and do not scale with demand. When software cannot scale, historically hardware often comes to the rescue. We perform the first reverse engineering of a compression accelerator--Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) microarchitecture and--find different amount of time on each, a novel data structure-dependent property. Using this information, we then build Lasso, a low-cost, high-performance detector for AI-generated content that turns the accelerator into a measuring instrument. For text detection, Lasso achieves 100% accuracy on original DetectRL text and retains 92% average accuracy after paraphrasing, compared with 78% for Binoculars and 55% for DetectGPT. Across original, paraphrased, and perturbed text, it achieves 82% average accuracy, outperforming all five baselines. With topic, length, and formatting matched, accuracy reaches 95% for instruction-tuned generators, including when the tested generator is unseen. On RAID, accuracy averages 82% when trained on one generator and tested on another, and 74% across eight held-out domains. Detection takes 0.74 microseconds, a speedup of at least 83,784x across five baselines. At the same time, Lasso consumes over 99% less energy per document than both Binoculars and DetectGPT. At the same time, Lasso detects AI-generated videos, software code, and images with 67.5%, 70% and 78% accuracy, respectively, with low latency and power opening avenues for practical real time and edge device detection of multimodality AI artifacts for the first time. No other compared technique supports detection across all four modalities: text, video, images, and code.

Valavan Manohararajah, Vithursan Thangarasa
Generating a token with a language model requires a fixed amount of arithmetic, whose energy sets a floor beneath any hardware. For Qwen3-1.7B at a 16K-token context, gate-level measurements at 5 nm place this floor at 0.89 mJ per token, yet an NVIDIA B300 spends 391-1,120x that. The excess is the price of generality, software layers, programmable hardware and moving weights and key-value (KV) caches from external memory, and it widens with each process generation. We present a co-design approach that brings token generation close to this floor and then lowers the floor itself, optimizing silicon and model together in a gate-level search loop. Fixing one model architecture in the datapath, with weights still loadable, and holding weights and every conversation's KV cache on-die, a pre-silicon 5 nm design brings an unchanged Qwen3-1.7B token to 3.4x its floor. Co-designing the model with the circuits at fixed quality lowers the floor to 0.29 mJ and the token to 0.52 mJ, 1.8x the new floor and less than the baseline model's arithmetic alone, while on-die capacity grows from one user to twelve. Against a measured B300 serving the same twelve users, the design decodes each user's tokens 110x faster at 690x lower energy. To show that one fixed architecture can serve, as a co-processor, the latency-critical workloads around a frontier model, we introduce Polyglot-DC (1.7B and 4B, each with its own design), specialized for each job by distillation and task-specific training into its own weights. As a drafter it speeds single-user speculative decoding of large open models by up to 6.6x at the maximum reasoning effort. Its guard returns multilingual verdicts in a millisecond or less, within a point of the strongest open guard. Its agent and financial-reasoning models lead comparable open models on established benchmarks, with a reasoning turn falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds.

♻ ☆ AdaptViT: Runtime-Adaptive Vision Transformer Deployment on Custom RISC-V CEC
Vishnu PS, Ajay Kumar M, Yike Li, Robert Bogdan Staszewski, Deepu John
Deploying Vision Transformers (ViTs) on low-power edge devices is challenging due to high computational demands. Conventional pruning frameworks require a separate compiled binary for each sparsity level, increasing storage overhead and limiting runtime adaptability. This paper presents an end-to-end deployment pipeline that transforms pretrained ViTs into a single runtime-configurable binary, enabling dynamic compute-budget switching on embedded CPUs. This is achieved by restructuring generated C kernels with modified loop bounds and binary-mask control logic, allowing execution to switch across discrete sparsity levels via compact external configuration files. Compared to multi-binary deployment, the proposed runtime-adaptive approach reduces on-device storage by up to 4.86x, requiring only 163 MB for ViT-Base instead of nearly 800 MB. To maximize pruning efficiency, we introduce a hardware-aligned block pruning strategy for Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) layers. In addition, a custom ISA extension is proposed to exploit input-reuse patterns in linear projection kernels. On a Synopsys TRV32P3FX RISC-V processor, the full system achieves up to 2.8x speedup at 65% MLP and 50% attention-head pruning for ViT-Base. The ISA extension alone provides a 1.56x speedup and 33% lower inference energy, with a 24.7% area overhead in a TSMC 28 nm implementation.

♻ ☆ LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
Arnab Sanyal, Gourav Datta, Sandeep P. Chinchali
Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a 4 GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an 8 GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, llama.cpp's K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. LazyWeights keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At 1% and 3.5% perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are 5.7-31.4% smaller than the best llama.cpp format. A bit-exact 0.21 mm^2 ASIC decoder unit (1 GHz, 7 nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to 36% and 38% (54% and 44% with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, LazyWeights needs 58-64% less time and 53-57% less energy per token than CPU llama.cpp, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6x faster at 3.89 bits per weight. Across RTLLM v2.0 modules, the approach consistently yields post-synthesis gains under fixed commercial synthesis tool call budgets, and ablations confirm that reward-guided selection and candidate dropping are central to sample-efficient progress. Emerging CPU matrix engines, such as Intel AMX, enable high throughput by batching multiple queries. However, they support only low-precision formats, which can significantly degrade recall (i.e., search quality). Specifically, KatoANN represents each vector using a 16-bit code, splits it into high- and low-byte planes, and computes near-exact distances using 8-bit matrix multiplications that the matrix engine supports. To reduce extra multiplication overhead, it ranks all candidates by their high bytes alone and refines only a few survivors with the full distance. KatoANN also reduces memory footprint since it does not maintain a full-precision copy of the vectors. We implement a KatoANN prototype on Intel AMX. Our experimental results show that KatoANN outperforms existing partition-based systems across the high-recall range.

The same ProtoLang program can both drive and monitor transactions. Users specify RTL communication protocols as succinct imperative programs. To alleviate this, prior work has developed automated uncomputation synthesis based on a computational-basis formulation of ancilla use. However, this formulation is tailored to classically structured ancilla computations. For more general circuits, it may be undefined, yield unintended functionality, or fail to synthesize uncomputation. It therefore falls short of providing a precise and general formulation of uncomputation beyond classical ancilla use. To address these limitations, we propose a new formulation of ancilla use that specifies the operation of each gate through two complementary aspects: (1) the functionality it implements and (2) the transformation it induces on ancilla roles. Based on this specification, we define uncomputation as restoring the initial ancilla role while implementing the identity functionality. This perspective enables a simple Use-first strategy for automatically synthesizing uncomputation in cases both within and beyond the scope of prior approaches. We further develop a complete inference system for reasoning about specifications, together with a derivation-directed procedure for automatically synthesizing efficient uncomputation, enabling systematic uncomputation synthesis even in challenging cases beyond the scope of our automatic strategy.

We prove that weakest-precondition equations for loops have unique solutions in the parameterized predicate domain. Dynamic partial-order reduction (DPOR) has emerged as a promising approach to addressing interleaving explosion in bounded model checking of concurrent programs. Given an equivalence relation on interleavings, the model checker explores a program's executions while minimizing repeated visits to the same class; optimal model checkers avoid such repetition altogether. A coarser equivalence promises faster exploration by reducing the number of classes. This has motivated alternatives to Mazurkiewicz's trace equivalence such as reads-from and reads-value-from equivalence. This promise, however, does not always materialize in practice: while a coarser equivalence can yield exponentially fewer classes on some families of programs, it may offer little or no reduction for the program at hand. We show how to quantify the advantage of coarser equivalences for individual programs. We focus on the problem of counting the reads-from (RF) equivalence classes induced by a given program, as well as the problem of computing the ratio of RF to Mazurkiewicz class counts under sequential consistency. We show that both problems are $\#\mathrm{P}$-hard and that the reduction ratio remains hard to approximate accurately under standard complexity assumptions. Guided by these limits, we present CoEst, a sampling-based algorithm for estimating both the RF count and its ratio to the Mazurkiewicz count. For a fixed number of threads, each trial runs in polynomial time and yields unbiased count estimates. As the number of independent trials grows, the count and ratio estimates converge almost surely to their true values. Our algorithm can provide statistical evidence for deciding whether Mazurkiewicz or RF model checking is likely to be faster for a given program. In experiments across 34 benchmark configurations, our method selects the faster checker in 99.4% of runs using a one-minute estimation budget.

Across the evaluated GPU thread configurations, SIMTurn introduces only 17-24% scheduler-area overhead relative to IPDOM, compared with 39-91% for ITS, and stays within 8% of IPDOM on workloads that never need cross-subgroup progress. On kernels with genuine cross-subgroup parallelism, SIMTurn tracks ITS closely and is up to 2.7x faster than a software-serialized IPDOM baseline.

This process forces researchers to grapple with the reality that a matrix expressible as one equation on paper can map to thousands of bit-level quantum logic gates, historically written by hand. Even worse, it often ends with a discovery that the needed resources grow so quickly with matrix size that the quantum algorithm loses its asymptotic speedup. In this work, we present MARBLE, a language that automatically synthesizes an efficient circuit from the publication-style formula for the entries of a matrix. MARBLE algebraically rewrites programs into symbolic combinations of simpler matrices that have known circuit realizations. It then emits an OpenQASM circuit and certifies whether its cost is poly-logarithmic in problem size, as required by quantum algorithms. When evaluated on quantum applications ranging from fluid dynamics to physical Hamiltonians, MARBLE matches or surpasses 37 of 39 published baselines. On the low end, it automatically matches many theoretically optimal circuits, and on the high end, it improves on a published construction in fluid dynamics by 10,487x in subnormalization. MARBLE produces exponentially smaller circuits than the leading tool FABLE, and it successfully compiles matrices whose dimensions exceed 2^100 within five seconds on a laptop.

Aggressive compiler optimization today occupies two distant extremes. We introduce solver-based super-analysis, a middle ground that uses expensive SMT-based analysis while transformations remain conventional, avoiding program synthesis entirely. The key argument for super-analysis is that conventional compilers have rich transformation rules, but proving them to be safe requires complex reasoning: proving a safety check dead often needs facts from three independent LLVM analyses simultaneously, a conjunctive entailment problem suited to an SMT solver, not to any single dataflow pass. In a factored layout, a traversal can focus on relevant fields and ignore the rest, similar to extracting a column from a SoA representation; in this setting, traversals over scalar fields can be vectorized. Working with raw byte arrays is error-prone, though: wrong indexing can silently read bytes from a wrong field or write past the end of a value. We therefore introduce SoCal, a type-safe language for expressing traversals over factored ADTs. Our compiler, Colobus, transforms a simple functional language with ADTs reminiscent of Haskell to C, using SoCal as the intermediate representation. Colobus generates traversals over byte arrays in the factored representation and performs optimizations such as field skipping and vectorization. Across a suite of benchmarks, Colobus shows the average speedups of 3.8x and 5.2x over fold and map passes, respectively.

♻ ☆ CrypTorch: Unified PyTorch-based Auto-tuning Compiler for Private Machine Learning Inference

Our characterization study finds that the performance of state-of-the-art MPC frameworks is often dominated by operator-approximation strategies, where ML operators not natively supported by MPC are replaced with iterative methods or polynomials. At the core of CrypTorch is its auto-tuning stage, which extracts cost estimates from the target MPC backend and quality estimates from a proxy PyTorch execution, and uses them to automatically select a set of approximations that maximizes performance while satisfying the given quality constraint. We show that CrypTorch's auto-tuner improves performance across multiple MPC backends by 1.14--1.60x without degrading accuracy, and by 1.17--1.92x with less than 3% accuracy degradation. CrypTorch's unified design also improves programmability and usability by allowing multiple backends to share other common compiler functionality and optimizations. This is closely related to the classical concept of backward error in numerical analysis, which allows an algorithm to return a solution to an arbitrary perturbation of the problem. Despite the qualitative similarity of these concepts, we show that they can exhibit large quantitative differences. Notably, we prove that, while a linear system with any $n \times n$ matrix $A$ can be solved to backward error $ε$ using $O(\log(n) / ε)$ matrix-vector products with $A$, any algorithm that solves a random $ε$-sized perturbation of $A$ requires $Ω(n)$ matrix-vector products. This means that a useful perturbation for solving a linear system in backward error must be adaptive to the input. Interestingly, however, randomness is still essential: we show that any deterministic method that attains small backward error for all linear systems provably requires $Ω(n)$ matrix-vector products, resulting in the first separation between randomized and deterministic algorithms in a natural computational model for solving linear systems. Finally, we show that matrix structure can significantly affect backward error complexity. For example, we show a deterministic $O(1/ε)$ matrix-vector product algorithm for symmetric linear systems.

Without extra centers, the exact approximation ratio is $2(1+H_{k-1})$ (also in Euclidean space), improving the previous upper bound by a factor of $2$ ($H_j$ denotes the $j$th harmonic number). This tight analysis reveals that even one extra center improves the approximation ratio by an additive $Θ(\log\log k)$, whereas previous bounds show no improvement. For every $\ell>0$, our analysis gives upper bounds with the same dependence on $k$ and $Δ$ as our tight bound for metric $k$-median, with leading constants depending only on $\ell$ and whether the metric is Euclidean. Beyond the improved dependence on $Δ$, our leading constants are smaller than those in previous analyses. In particular, for the widely used Euclidean $k$-means objective, our upper bound without extra centers is $(1+\varphi)(1+H_{k-1})$, where $\varphi\approx1.618$ is the golden ratio, improving upon the previous constant of $5$. With oversampling, a constant fraction of extra centers is known to provide a constant-factor approximation. For example, with $10\%$ extra centers, our guarantee is $5.7$, compared with the best previous guarantee of $25.9$.
comment: 46 pages, 2 figures
☆ A Common Improved Bound for Asymmetric TSP and Path TSP
MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Changki Yun
We give polynomial-time $(R_*+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for asymmetric TSP and asymmetric path TSP, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, where $R_*=6+\sqrt2+\sqrt{15+6\sqrt2}\approx12.2604$. Both guarantees hold relative to the corresponding subtour relaxations, whose integrality ratios are therefore at most $R_*$. This improves the previous guarantees of below $14.7$ for asymmetric TSP and $15$ for asymmetric path TSP [Vygen, 2026]. Our algorithms strengthen subtour covers and recursive augmentation in the laminar framework [Svensson, Tarnawski, Vegh, JACM'20; Traub, Vygen, 2025]. The recursive analysis retains the paths through contracted regions and accounts jointly for their cost and the dual mass they visit. We also improve the reduction from asymmetric path TSP to vertebrate pairs [Traub, Vygen, 2025] by comparing two initial walks with complementary completion bounds. Applied to Vygen's existing vertebrate-pair algorithm, this reduction alone improves the path factor from $15$ to below $14.7$, matching his asymmetric TSP guarantee.
☆ A Framework for Cost-Preserving Rounding with Applications to Laminar Thin Trees
Jannis Blauth, Rico Zenklusen
In the context of finding thin trees, like laminarly-thin trees or globally-thin trees, it turned out to be challenging to round a fractional solution to an integral one without losing cost, while only having a constant-factor violation of the thinness constraints. We provide a general framework for this problem, in a much broader context, that reduces the problem to finding a certain type of rounding algorithm with only an approximate prize guarantee. We show that, up to a change in constants, the rounding problem with approximate prize guarantee that we use is equivalent to the original question. As an application, we obtain a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a laminar constantly-thin tree of cost no higher than the one of the natural linear programming solution, thus obtaining the first result without cost loss of this type (even for the special case of chain-constrained trees). Moreover, our framework gives a new perspective on how to approach the problem of finding globally-thin trees without cost loss.
☆ Color Refinement Distinguishes Connected Rooted Outerplanar Graphs
Louann Coste, M{ó}nika Csik{ó}s, Laurent Viennot
Color refinement, also known as the $1$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm ($1$-WL), is a classical near-linear-time heuristic for graph isomorphism, which also captures the expressive power of message-passing graph neural networks. A long line of work asks on which graph classes $1$-WL, or its higher-dimensional variant $k$-WL, identifies every graph; the least such $k$ is the WL-dimension of the class. Planar graphs have WL-dimension at most $3$ (Kiefer, Ponomarenko and Schweitzer, 2019), and whether $2$-WL already distinguishes all planar graphs is a central open problem. We bring new insight on this question for outerplanar graphs, whose WL-dimension is $2$. We show that color refinement, i.e. 1-WL, distinguishes connected rooted outerplanar graphs: two non-isomorphic such graphs receive different stable colorings once a single vertex, the root, is individualized. The root is necessary, as there are non-isomorphic $2$-connected outerplanar graphs that color refinement does not distinguish. Our result extends to pseudo-rooted graphs, in which the stable coloring merely contains a singleton color class, and to non-connected graphs whose components all contain such a class. Consequently, the $(1,1)$-WL test of Rattan and Seppelt (2023) distinguishes all outerplanar graphs. We proceed by inversion: we reconstruct a connected rooted outerplanar graph, up to isomorphism, from its color graph, the weighted quotient of the graph by its stable color classes, together with its root color. The reconstruction runs in time linear in the output size and is canonical, which yields a near-linear-time canonization algorithm for these graphs. Our main tool is a dichotomy lemma, formalized in Rocq: in a rooted outerplanar graph with an equitable coloring, every block either receives pairwise distinct colors or admits a color-preserving mirror symmetry fixing its vertex closest to the root.
☆ How rigid is maximum cardinality search? Stability and locality of MCS orderings under edge updates, verified in Lean
Md Thoriqul Islam Thonmay, Gregory Morse
For which sets F of edge modifications do a graph G and the modified graph share a maximum cardinality search (MCS) ordering? We prove that they do whenever, along every proper common MCS prefix, each unchosen vertex's neighbour count in the second graph exceeds its count in the first by zero or one. In particular, inserting or deleting any matching, or flipping a single edge, preserves a common ordering, and under the same hypothesis every common MCS prefix extends to a full common ordering without backtracking. Neither part of the hypothesis can simply be dropped: inserting a triangle, a P_4 or a 2P_3 shows that the +1 bound cannot be relaxed to +2, and a disjoint mixed insert/delete pair shows that the one-directional condition is needed. For the canonical ordering (smallest-index tie-breaking) under a single-edge update, an insertion can first change the ordering only strictly between the endpoints' positions, and a deletion only at the later endpoint; when no break fires, the ordering is unchanged. A boolean-adjacency executable refines the abstract probe-then-repair update. All of these results, including the four obstructions, are proved in Lean 4 over Mathlib, re-checked by independent kernel checkers, and registered in the Palomar registry. On paper we further show that the first break of an insertion is located in O((deg(v)+1) log n) time, independent of the window length. We claim no worst-case asymptotic speedup over recomputation.
comment: 14 pages, 1 table. Code and proofs: https://github.com/thonmay/mcs-lean . Palomar registry: PALOMAR-2026-10-04-000009
☆ Exact-Quota Facility Location: A Transfer Framework and Three Approximation Guarantees
Hang Luo
Facility location with outliers asks which facilities to open and which clients to serve, subject to a prescribed service quota. We give a framework for transferring facility-location cost certificates to this exact-quota setting. The framework yields deterministic polynomial-time approximation guarantees of $571/376<1.52$ for metric facility location with outliers, strictly less than $1.853$ for priority facility location with outliers, and $2.16995<2.17$ for squared-metric facility location with outliers. Each algorithm serves the prescribed number of clients and pays the original facility-opening costs. The framework separates initialization from improvement. A growth process is stopped when it first reaches the quota; deleting excess clients from its last batch leaves a payment deficit supported on a bounded number of facilities. Greedy additions then reoptimize the served client set. A threshold-coverage representation makes the resulting service cost supermodular and allows the usual density analysis to compare different client sets. Finally, enumerating and prepaying a constant number of expensive facilities absorbs the exceptional costs. A transfer theorem states exactly which initialization certificate is sufficient and how many prepaid facilities it requires. The three applications supply this certificate in different ways. The metric case uses a quota prefix of reassigning JMS; the priority case uses persistent contributions and a cleanup ordered by service level; and the squared-metric case uses a local factor-revealing certificate valid for arbitrary client subsets of the same run. We provide complete finite proofs of the numerical interfaces, including an exact rational certificate for the squared-metric bound.
comment: 24 pages. Includes an exact rational certificate and a solver-free verifier as ancillary files
☆ The Complexity of Traffic Engineering in Segment Routing Networks
Matthias Bentert, Stefan Schmid
Segment routing is a modern variant of source routing which has recently become popular in the Internet. It allows operators to equip network packets with an additional header which specifies segments: a list of waypoints the packet needs to traverse on its way to the destination. This is reminiscent of Valiant routing in parallel computing and introduces an additional degree of freedom in traffic engineering. This flexibility can be exploited to minimize congestion in the network. This paper sheds light on the computational complexity of traffic engineering in segment routing networks. We consider two problem variants: a fixed-length variant where link weights are given and only waypoints can be chosen, and a variable-length variant where additionally the network operator can also choose the link weights, which then define the shortest paths taken between the waypoints. We prove that the first variant is NP-hard even if the network graph is planar and if all demands and link weights are 1. We also show that the second variant is NP-hard already for planar network graphs with all demands being 1. On the positive side, we present a compact and general mixed integer linear program to compute exact solutions for the first variant.
☆ Long rational and Gaussian integer multiplication
Yuval Spiizer, Raphael S. Steiner
Long integer multiplication is a fundamental operation in computational algebra, heavily relying on Toom--Cook and related evaluation-interpolation algorithms. Conventional wisdom dictates that multiplication on the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is reduced to standard rational integer multiplication, since $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is a ring extension of $\mathbb{Z}$. We show that this approach is far from optimal and moreover inverting this established paradigm, that is reducing rational to Gaussian multiplication, leads to faster rational integer multiplication algorithms. We introduce a novel Toom--Cook framework that reduces rational long integer multiplication to Gaussian integer multiplication, yielding a strictly more efficient computational pipeline. By taking advantage of the special properties of the rational integer domain inside the Gaussian integers, we achieve a more favourable algebraic structure that reduces the overall arithmetic cost in every metric. To validate this theoretical shift, we provide a complete implementation of our algorithm. Benchmarks demonstrate that our approach outperforms the highly optimised GNU Multiple Precision Arithmetic Library (GMP) by up to 29\%, bridging a fundamental theoretical insight with significant practical improvements in high-performance computer algebra.
comment: 38 pages
☆ Parameterized Approximation for Minimizing Uncovered Elements and Unsatisfied Constraints
Rudranarayan Kar, Souvik Saha, Abhishek Sahu
Min-UnCoverage asks for at most $k$ sets minimizing uncovered weight. Min-Unsat SAT and Min-Unsat CSP ask for an assignment with at most $k$ true variables minimizing the weight of unsatisfied clauses or constraints. For constraints of arity at most $d$, we give a deterministic $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Min-Unsat CSP in $(dk/\varepsilon)^{O(k)}N^{O(1)}$ time, where $N$ is the input size. This also gives approximation schemes for bounded-arity SAT and coverage with bounded element frequency. We show that weighted coverage with set size at most $d$ can be solved exactly in $2^{O(kd)}N^{O(1)}$ time by adapting color-coding. For coverage on incidence graphs of bounded semi-ladder index, we give a deterministic parameterized approximation scheme . We show that, unless $\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]$, SAT and CSP have no finite-factor FPT approximation parameterized by $k+d$ when variable frequency is at most $d$, or on $K_{3,3}$-free incidence graphs of semi-ladder index at most four. Known Hitting Set hardness gives the same lower bound for all three problems at VC dimension two. Under the same assumption, we show that no computable relaxation $g(k,d)\geq k$ allows an FPT algorithm to preserve a prescribed unsatisfied-weight target for SAT or CSP, already for arity three and, separately, bounded variable frequency. For coverage, known algorithms preserve the target using at most $k+1$ sets on incidence graphs of bounded semi-ladder index.
☆ Tight Quantum Query Bounds for Minimum Cut and Multicut on Dense Graphs
Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu
We determine the dense worst-case quantum query complexity of exact minimum multicut on simple unweighted undirected graphs. With at most $k$ explicit demand pairs, our adjacency-array algorithm uses $\OO(n+\min\{m,n^{3/2}\sqrt{k}\})$ queries; a matching lower bound holds for every $1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and sufficiently large $n$, with constants uniform in $k$. In particular, the $k=1$ case gives an $\OO(n^{3/2})$ query algorithm for prescribed $s$--$t$ cut. The upper bound combines degree-sensitive spectral estimates of local improvement with refinement by unions of label classes. These steps retain every original optimum and permit exact acquisition without an additional label-count factor. Separately, we prove an $Ω(n^{3/2})$ global minimum-cut lower bound on dense connected graphs, matching the existing upper bound up to polylogarithmic factors. It holds for the value and for any optimum shore, even with known degrees and sorted neighbor arrays; regular hard instances have balanced optimum cuts. Both lower bounds use degree-preserving switches and classify optimum outputs across a hidden threshold. Our upper bound concerns input queries, not total running time: computation on acquired data may be exponential, even in the single-demand case. Matching bounds at each prescribed sparse edge count are not established.
☆ Exact Failure Probabilities for d-Choice Cuckoo Hashing
Chenyang Zhang, Ling Ren
In d-choice cuckoo hashing, each of n items must be placed in one of its d candidate slots in a table of M slots, and every slot holds at most one item. We give a polynomial-time dynamic programming algorithm to compute the exact probability that no valid placement exists. Our method also handles the variant with separate tables.
☆ A PTAS for Euclidean Capacitated Vehicle Routing
Zachary Friggstad, Fabrizio Grandoni, Ramin Mousavi, Kinter Ren, Mohammad R. Salavatipour
In the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), introduced by Dantzig and Ramser in 1959, we are given an $n$-node graph $G=(V,E)$ with metric edges costs $c(e)$, a depot $r\in V$, and an integer vehicle capacity $Q$. The goal is to find a minimum-cost collection of tours, each containing the depot and visiting at most other $Q$ nodes, such that the tours cover all the nodes. In this paper we focus on the Euclidean CVRP problem, where the nodes represent points on $\mathbb{R}^2$, and the edge costs are the respective Euclidean distances. Euclidean CVRP generalizes the classical NP-hard Euclidean TSP problem (the special case with $Q=n-1$), that admits a PTAS [Arora FOCS'96/Mitchell SODA'96]. A long-standing open problem has been generalizing the latter PTAS to Euclidean CVRP. A polynomial-time $(2+ε)$-approximation for this problem follows from the PTAS for Euclidean TSP and the tour-partitioning technique for CVRP [Haimovich, Kan Math. OR'85]. This was the best known until a recent improvement of the approximation factor to slightly below 2 [Friggstad, Grandoni, Mousavi SODA'26]. There have been a series of papers presenting improved QPTASs by Das and Mathieu [SODA'10] (time $n^{\log^{O(1/ε)}n}$), Jayaprakash and Salavatipour [SODA'22] (time $n^{O_ε(\log^6 n)}$), and recently Sitters [ArXiV'25] (time $n^{O_ε(\log\log n)}$). In this paper, we solve the mentioned long-standing open problem by presenting a PTAS for Euclidean CVRP.
♻ ☆ A Fine-Grained Classification of Subquadratic Patterns for Subgraph Listing and Friends
Karl Bringmann, Egor Gorbachev
In an $m$-edge host graph $G$, all triangles can be listed in time $O(m^{1.5})$ [Itai, Rodeh '78], and all $k$-cycles can be listed in time $O(m^{2-1/{\lceil k/2 \rceil}} + t)$ where $t$ is the output size [Alon, Yuster, Zwick '97]. These classic results also hold for the colored problem variant, where the nodes of the host graph $G$ are colored by nodes in the pattern graph $H$, and we are only interested in subgraphs of $G$ that are isomorphic to the pattern $H$ and respect the colors. We study the problem of listing all $H$-subgraphs in the colored setting, for fixed pattern graphs $H$. As our main result, we determine all pattern graphs $H$ such that all $H$-subgraphs can be listed in subquadratic time $O(m^{2-\varepsilon} + t)$, where $t$ is the output size. Moreover, for each such subquadratic pattern $H$ we determine the smallest exponent $c(H)$ such that all $H$-subgraphs can be listed in time $O(m^{c(H)} + t)$. This is a vast generalization of the classic results on triangles and cycles. We also show the same results for two related problems: finding an $H$-subgraph of minimum total edge-weight in time $O(m^{c(H)})$, and enumerating all $H$-subgraphs in $O(m^{c(H)})$ preprocessing time and constant delay. Again we determine all pattern graphs $H$ that have complexity $c(H) < 2$, and for each such subquadratic pattern we determine the optimal complexity $c(H)$. To prove these results, we design new algorithms and prove conditional lower bounds based on standard hypotheses from fine-grained complexity theory. For our algorithms we introduce a new ingredient that we call hyper-degree splitting, where we split tuples of nodes into high degree and low degree depending on their number of common neighbors. This technique generalizes the classic high-degree-low-degree approach (which only splits along degrees of single nodes) and is crucial to obtain optimal algorithms.
